title: From Pixels to Paths: Cooperative AI for Autonomous Agricultural Navigation
affiliations: and Professor Jayashankar Telangana State Agricultural University (PJTSAU)

detail.title: From Pixels to Paths: Cooperative AI for Autonomous Agricultural Navigation
detail.abstract: Autonomous navigation in agricultural environments is constrained by unstructured terrain, crop variability, and limited sensing horizons. Conventional approaches relying solely on onboard sensors or satellite localization struggle to maintain robustness under real-world field conditions. This paper presents a cooperative artificial intelligence framework that distributes perception and control across heterogeneous agents. An aerial agent constructs a global semantic representation of the agricultural field, while a ground robot executes local navigation using this shared context. By framing autonomy as a coordinated perception-execution problem, the proposed system improves navigation accuracy, stability, and task completion reliability. Extensive simulation experiments and realistic field-inspired evaluations validate the effectiveness of the approach.

title: A Blessing in Disguise: How DeFi Hacks Trigger Unintended Liquidity Injections into US Money Markets

detail.title: A Blessing in Disguise: How DeFi Hacks Trigger Unintended Liquidity Injections into US Money Markets
detail.abstract: Do vulnerabilities in Decentralized Finance (DeFi) destabilize traditional short term funding markets? While the prevailing "Contagion Hypothesis" posits that the liquidation of stablecoin reserves triggers fire-sale spirals that transmit dis tress to traditional markets , we document a robust "Flight-to-Quality" effect to the contrary. In the wake of major DeFi exploits, spreads on 3-month AA-rated commercial paper (CP) exhibit a paradoxical narrowing. We identify a "liquidity recycling" mechanism driving this outcome: capital fleeing DeFi protocols is re intermediated into the traditional financial system via Prime Money Market Funds (MMFs) , where strict regulatory constraints (e.g., SEC Rule 2a-7) compel these funds to purchase high-quality paper. Our estimates indicate that this institutional demand shock quantitatively overwhelms the supply shock driven by stablecoin issuer redemptions. Rather than acting as vectors of financial contagion , these crypto native shocks serve as an inadvertent "safety valve" in segmented markets , providing transient liquidity support and effectively subsidizing borrowing costs for high-grade issuers in the real economy

title: Increasing Resettlement of Desert Areas: The Conquest of Arid Environments Between Natural Constraints and Human Determination

detail.title: Increasing Resettlement of Desert Areas: The Conquest of Arid Environments Between Natural Constraints and Human Determination
detail.abstract: Arid and semi-arid regions, long considered marginal and inhospitable, are increasingly targeted for agricultural expansion, resource development, and new urban settlements. This dissertation analyzes the growing trend of resettlement in desert environments by examining the interplay between natural constraints, technological innovations, socio-political dynamics, and sustainable planning strategies. Drawing on comparative case studies from North Africa, the Sahel, Kenya, and the Horn of Africa, the research identifies the principal drivers of desert reoccupation—demographic pressure, land saturation in fertile zones, state-led planning policies, and the emergence of new energy and agricultural frontiers. The study highlights the structural limits imposed by arid environments, including extreme water scarcity, dependence on fossil aquifers, fragile soils, recurrent droughts, and accelerating land degradation. These constraints undermine large-scale agricultural projects and heighten societal vulnerabilities, particularly for pastoral communities whose mobility is increasingly restricted. Yet, the analysis also shows that sustainability remains attainable when development pathways integrate adaptive governance, community-based resource management, efficient water-use technologies, and diversified economic strategies. Innovations such as managed aquifer recharge, solar-powered irrigation, desalination, and circular agriculture demonstrate the growing technical feasibility of inhabiting desert regions. However, their long-term viability depends on robust institutional coordination, respect for ecological limits, and participatory governance frameworks. The dissertation concludes that resettlement of desert areas is not only technically possible but strategically necessary for several states; nevertheless, its success ultimately hinges on the capacity to manage hydrological constraints, strengthen social resilience, and adopt integrated land–water planning approaches adapted to environmental variability.

title: Natural Methods to Protect Trees Against Large Herbivores: A Systematic Map of Research
affiliations: University of Southampton, University of Southampton, Forest Research, Alice Holt Lodge, University of Reading,  and University of Southampton

detail.title: Natural Methods to Protect Trees Against Large Herbivores: A Systematic Map of Research
detail.abstract: Tree planting initiatives have increased globally to address climate change and biodiversity loss, and improve human wellbeing, yet planting success is increasingly challenged by high densities of large herbivores that inhibit tree growth and survival. Conventional protection methods such as fencing, lethal control, and the use of plastic tree guards, are often costly, socially contentious, and environmentally unsustainable. Demand to find cost-effective and sustainable methods to tree protection is increasing. Natural tree protection methods (NTPMs), including the use of nurse plants, woody debris, and hedges may offer a sustainable solution to mitigate herbivory while providing additional ecological and social benefits. However, evidence of their effectiveness is highly variable, likely influenced by contextual and methodological factors such as herbivore species, target tree species, landscape characteristics, and study design. To clarify these uncertainties, we aim to produce a systematic map through collating, organising, and categorising knowledge cluster and gaps on the applications of different NTPMs in temperate regions. Literature searches will be conducted in English, using relevant search scientific databases (ISI Web of Science, Scopus, and ProQuest). Search terms will be defined by a primary question: What evidence exists on the application of natural tree protection methods for protecting target plants against large herbivore browsing? Information extracted from primary studies will include the NTPM species, the NTPM application (NTPM height, distance from target plant, study design, outcome measures, study location, and study duration). Results will be presented visually to summarise key features of the evidence base and identify knowledge gaps and clusters.

detail.abstract: Small firms in climate-vulnerable economies are under growing pressure to adopt climatesmart business models while operating within fragmented and weak entrepreneurial ecosystems. Yet the mechanisms through which education, individual capabilities and institutional conditions jointly shape climate-smart SME development remain insufficiently understood. This study introduces epistemic change as a transformation in entrepreneurs' underlying knowledge systems and interpretive schemas as a central cognitive mechanism enabling climate-smart venture development and green industrial upgrading. Using survey data from 300 climate-smart SMEs in Cameroon, the study applies multiple regression and Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling to test a hybrid framework integrating transformative learning, entrepreneurial cognition and entrepreneurial ecosystem perspectives. The findings show that entrepreneurship education affects venture performance only indirectly through epistemic change, while entrepreneurial personality traits and support from conventional businesses exert strong indirect effects via the same mechanism. Ecosystem support positively moderates the epistemic change-performance relationship, indicating that cognitive transformation translates into improved outcomes most effectively under supportive financial, regulatory and infrastructural conditions. The study advances small business strategy and development research by identifying epistemic change as a key mechanism linking learning, ecosystem alignment and climate-smart SME growth in emerging economies.

title: Addressing Anti-Competitive Practices in Bangladesh: Gaps in the institutional and Statutory Framework

detail.title: Addressing Anti-Competitive Practices in Bangladesh: Gaps in the institutional and Statutory Framework
detail.abstract: Anti-competitive practices are business or government practices that prevent or reduce competition in a market. Antitrust laws differ among state and federal laws to ensure businesses do not engage in competitive practices that harm other, usually smaller, businesses or consumers. These laws are formed to promote healthy competition within a free market by limiting the abuse of monopoly power. Competition allows companies to compete in order for products and services to improve; promote innovation; and provide more choices for consumers. In order to obtain greater profits, some large enterprises take advantage of market power to hinder the survival of new entrants. Anti-competitive practices are commonly only deemed illegal when the practice results in a substantial dampening in competition, hence why for a firm to be punished for any form of anti-competitive behaviour they generally need to be a monopoly or a dominant firm in a duopoly or oligopoly who has significant influence over the market.

detail.abstract: Political Humanism is a contemporary moral philosophy and governance theory that integrates ethics, institutional design, and macroeconomic reasoning around a single evaluative principle: the maximisation of human flourishing. Departing from the traditional left-right ideological spectrum, Political Humanism begins with an analysis of the individual's relationship to society and the state, derives a normative obligation to maximise collective well-being, and operationalises this obligation through a structured set of measurable outcomes-the Human Wellbeing Indices (HWix12). Situating itself within the humanist and utilitarian traditions, and drawing on contemporary capability-based and wellbeing-oriented approaches to political evaluation, Political Humanism is presented here as a post-ideological framework for democratic governance in the twenty-first century. The paper outlines the philosophical foundations of the framework, its institutional implications, and its relevance to ongoing debates in political philosophy, governance theory, and political economy.

title: Devotion Without Action: Islam, Charity, and Poverty in Comparative Perspective

detail.title: Devotion Without Action: Islam, Charity, and Poverty in Comparative Perspective

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors have no conflicts of interest to declare.

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether strong religious commitment in Islamic societies translates into lower poverty levels. Despite Islamic teachings that emphasize poverty alleviation through obligations like zakāt, our crosscountry analysis (2010-2019) finds no significant difference in poverty rates or individual charitable giving between Islamic and non-Islamic countries. Using covariate balancing propensity score matching, we control for observable differences and find that Islamic governments, particularly those with religious regimes, provide significantly less support to the poor. These findings suggest a gap between religious ideals and practical outcomes: while Muslims report high levels of religiosity, this does not lead to greater financial sacrifice or stateled poverty alleviation. Our study contributes to the ongoing debate on whether religion primarily serves a psychological and identity-based function, or whether devout individuals internalize and act upon the broader moral and economic commitments prescribed by their faith.

title: Investment Management Practices and Islamic Finance Efficiency: Evidence from Shahjalal Islami Bank Limited (Bangladesh)

detail.title: Investment Management Practices and Islamic Finance Efficiency: Evidence from Shahjalal Islami Bank Limited (Bangladesh)
detail.abstract: This paper evaluates the investment management efficiency of Shahjalal Islami Bank Limited (SJIBL), Mirsharai Branch, over 2020-2022. Combining branch-level records from an internship with SJIBL annual reports and Bangladesh Bank statistics, we quantify how deposit inflows are transformed into Shariah-compliant investments and their resulting impact on return on investment (ROI). The study uses both descriptive and econometric methods to measure portfolio concentration through the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI), estimate the relationship between deposits, investments, and ROI, and calculate a Sharpe-like risk-adjusted performance indicator (Sharpe 1966). Results reveal robust deposit growth and improved investment utilization, yet a relatively high concentration (HHI ≈ 0.55) in Bai-Muajjal and HPSM financing modes. This concentration is associated with lower ROI efficiency, suggesting that diversification into participatory contracts such as Mudaraba and Musharaka could enhance both profitability and risk sharing. The paper provides a branch-level efficiency diagnostic that integrates Islamic finance principles, emphasizing the alignment of profitability with maqasid al-shariah-promoting welfare, justice, and equitable distribution (Khan 2017, Ahmed 2015).

title: Desire, Display and Hidden Work: Consumerism and Commodity Fetishism in Dhaka

detail.title: Desire, Display and Hidden Work: Consumerism and Commodity Fetishism in Dhaka
detail.abstract: This paper studies how consumerism and commodity fetishism shape everyday life in Dhaka. The focus is on the young generation who buy and show branded goods and on garment workers who make many of those goods. The main claim is that strong desire for brands is taught daily by ads, apps and festivals and this desire often hides the labor and hardship behind the products. Short city observations and two composite voices (one young buyer, one factory worker) are used as primary material and are connected to ideas from Marx, Baudrillard, Adorno and Horkheimer, Bhattacharya and recent Bangladeshi research. In Dhaka, the case is unique because the buyer and the maker live in the same metro area, yet their lives rarely meet. Overall, the findings show that brand desire and smooth digital retail create strong peer pressure among the young generation, while the same system keeps workers invisible, widens moral distance and normalizes inequality across the city.

detail.abstract:
The PSID Geospatial Data provide the geographic codes necessary to link individual and family data from the PSID in each year to contextual data from secondary sources such as the Census and American Community Survey (ACS). The PSID Geospatial Data are available in the restricted data enclave and are the most requested restricted files. Over the course of the study, geocoding has been conducted using five different Censuses (see the online Geospatial File Description). Addresses are geocoded to the relevant Census geographic identifiers (e.g., starting with the 2011 wave, address information has been geocoded to the 2010 census geographic identifiers). 

In 2019, a new geocoding procedure was initiated to prioritize the use of the physical address of PSID respondents’ residences. During the past several waves (2005-2017), it was determined that for a small subset of cases the U.S. postal mailing address provided by the respondent for the mailing of their interview incentive payment was used to determine the geocode, even when a different physical address was provided earlier in the interview. The current 2019 geocoding process was updated to use the postal mail address only when there is no physical address.1 The new design for the geocode file (physical address first) will be available for approved users in the enclave and will include the updated address; a previous version (old design, mailing address first) that includes the original addresses will also be available in the enclave for comparison. 

This technical note describes the differences in the geocoded locations using this new process (physical address) compared to the previous process (mailing address for some). For the 2005- 2017 PSID waves about 3% of families obtained a geocode based on their mailing address. While these families are more likely to move, the overall migration rates using their physical address were not statistically different that those using the mailing address. In addition, the families that previously had a geocoded mailing address have different characteristics than those where a physical address was used. Evaluating the characteristics of the Census tracts where these families live, using either their physical address or the mailing address, does not yield statistically significant different mean estimates for a variety of tract or county characteristics. Overall, the impact on estimates of using this new geocoding procedure is minimal.

title: Design Principles for Transparent and Sovereign Public Systems: A Cross-Sector Framework for Democratic, Financial, Resource, and Digital Governance

detail.abstract: Modern states increasingly rely on complex, opaque systems to allocate political power, financial capital, natural resources, and digital data. Across these domains, structural weaknessesdefault allocation without explicit consent, delayed transparency, and misaligned incentivesundermine legitimacy and efficiency. This paper identifies recurring patterns in governance failures and proposes a unified framework to improve transparency, accountability, and systemic resilience. The framework preserves private enterprise, does not restrict lawful activity, and relies on consent-based triggers, disclosure obligations, and competitive mechanisms.

detail.abstract: Social media has become an integral part of daily life for young adults, influencing not only communication but also perceptions of self and mental well-being. This exploratory study examines the impact of social media use on self-esteem, social comparison, body image, and mental health among young adults. A mixed-method approach was employed, collecting data through an online survey completed by 40 participants. Quantitative data were gathered using Likert-scale questions assessing social comparison, anxiety, body image concerns, and life satisfaction, while qualitative responses explored participants' personal experiences and perceptions. Findings indicate that higher social media usage is associated with increased social comparison and anxiety, alongside fluctuations in self-esteem and body satisfaction. Qualitative analysis revealed recurring themes of pressure to appear perfect and feelings of inadequacy when comparing oneself with peers online. These results suggest that social media has a measurable effect on psychological well-being and highlight the need for awareness and strategies to mitigate negative impacts. This study provides insights for future research and interventions targeting young adults' mental health in the digital era.

title: A seven-day allied health model of care in an acute hospital trauma population: an implementation study
affiliations: , , , , , , , University of Melbourne - Royal Melbourne Hospital,  and

detail.title: A seven-day allied health model of care in an acute hospital trauma population: an implementation study
detail.abstract: ObjectiveDespite one-third of all trauma admissions occurring over the weekend in Australia, most acute trauma patients only receive allied health input within traditional Monday to Friday service models. This study aimed to determine the acceptability, fidelity and feasibility of a new seven-day allied health model of care within one of Australia’s busiest trauma hospitals.MethodsAn implementation study evaluated the commencement of a new model of care with an additional seven full-time-equivalent, predominantly senior, allied health clinicians over seven days. Acceptability was evaluated through surveys completed by medical, nursing and allied health staff working in the trauma service (n=151), pre- and post-implementation. Fidelity was evaluated by reviewing referral response time, weekend occasions of service, and at pre-implementation (n=484 patients), 6-months (n=456) and 18-months (n=532) post-implementation. Feasibility was evaluated through practicality and limited efficacy testing (changes in length of stay and Monday discharges) using the Mann-Whitney U or chi-squared tests.ResultsSurvey results indicated improved accessibility, adequacy, and continuity of staffing. Recruitment and work-life balance were cited as practical challenges. There were significant reductions in referral response times across allied health (from median 17.0 [IQR 6.0- 25.0] hours to median 12.0 [5.0-21.0] hours, p<0.001), a 53% increase in weekend occasions of service, and although length of stay remained unchanged, the proportion of Monday discharges increased (13% to 18%, p=0.02).ConclusionA seven-day allied health trauma service was successfully implemented with outcomes indicating it will be sustainable. Findings are useful for scalability to other hospitals and clinical specialties.

detail.abstract:
This technical report uses data from the Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID) Short-Term Coresidents module administered during the 2003 Core interview to describe reported short-term coresidence in PSID family units since 2001. Since these data were collected, research in family demography has increasingly emphasized the dynamic quality of family composition and the frequent occurrence but brief duration of some types of living arrangements, including cohabitation, coresidence with extended kin, and doubled-up households. The purpose of this report is to describe the observed prevalence and duration of short-term coresidence reported in PSID at one wave so that users may assess to what extent dynamic family living arrangements are potentially underestimated when this information is not collected.

The report includes four parts: (1) estimated prevalence and duration of short-term coresidence in family units; (2) social and demographic characteristics of family units that experienced short- term coresidence in comparison to those that did not; (3) demographic characteristics of the individuals who were short-term coresidents; and (4) estimates of the prevalence and duration of cohabiting unions over the two-year period with and without taking short-term coresidence into account.

publicationDetails.detailsText: University of Milan Bicocca Department of Economics, Management and Statistics Working Paper No. 566

detail.abstract: We consider a medium-scale macroeconomic model where the zero lower bound on interest rates remains binding permanently. We estimate the model for the Japanese economy, encompassing both active and passive fiscal policy scenarios. Our findings reveal a predominantly passive fiscal policy stance during the period spanning from 1995 to 2023. We compute fiscal multipliers for various policy instruments, showing that under the backdrop of passive fiscal policy: i) multipliers are lower than in an active fiscal policy regime; ii) government spending multipliers remain below one; iii) tax reductions can be associated with a decrease in output and inflation. A counterfactual analysis suggests that a more active fiscal policy would have resulted in a higher price level without increasing output volatility.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Greece Working Paper No. 354

detail.abstract: Using a panel of 116 advanced, emerging market and developing economies over the period 1990-2022, we examine the direct effects of natural disasters on economic activity and public finances and the medium-term effects of post-natural disaster reconstruction, through public spending, on economic activity. As anticipated, we find that natural disasters negatively affect both economic activity and public finances with the output effects being more pronounced in the case of extreme vis-à-vis major natural disasters. Employing a panel local projection methodology combined with an instrumental variable approach, and after conducting a series of robustness checks to address endogeneity concerns, the results reveal that reconstruction spending can serve as an effective driver of medium-term growth. Specifically, a 1% increase in real cyclically adjusted government expenditure following an extreme natural disaster leads to a 2.49% increase in real output five years after the shock. Moreover, the effects of reconstruction spending are found to be stronger in countries with lower public debt, lower trade openness, higher financial development, fixed exchange rate regimes, emerging market rather than advanced or least developed economies, countries with higher old-age dependency ratios, and lower agricultural or tourism dependence.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how governance and education affect VAT compliance in 25 EU nations between 2008 and 2022. The dependent variable is the VAT gap, which is the difference between expected and actual VAT revenue. GDP growth is included as a macroeconomic control, and governance metrics like regulatory quality and corruption control are examined alongside education indicators, such as primary, secondary, and tertiary enrollment. The research takes time and country-specific heterogeneity into account using fixed effects panel regression. According to the results, higher levels of education are linked to improved VAT compliance, indicating that education increases civic engagement and tax morale. While higher corruption is associated with increased VAT gaps, stronger regulations also improve compliance. Additionaly, the findings show the way human capital, institutional quality, and economic conditions interact to shape fiscal outcomes. Findings further provide policymakers evidence that integrating social and institutional strategies can increase tax collection and decrease tax evasion.

title: Transfer Learning in Spatiotemporal Graph Neural Networks for Traffic Forecasting: Taxonomy, Analysis, and Future Directions

detail.title: Transfer Learning in Spatiotemporal Graph Neural Networks for Traffic Forecasting: Taxonomy, Analysis, and Future Directions

declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported by the International Graduate School of Science and Engineering (IGSSE) of the Technical University of Munich (TUM), through the MINDMAP project

detail.abstract: Accurate traffic forecasting is vital for many intelligent transportation system applications. Graph neural network (GNN)-based spatiotemporal models achieve remarkable success by capturing the spatial dependencies among sensors and the temporal dynamics of traffic flow. However, these models rely heavily on large volumes of high-quality sensor data, limiting their applicability in data-scarce regions. Transfer learning offers a promising solution by enabling the reuse of knowledge learned from data-rich cities or road networks. In recent years, numerous transfer learning frameworks have been proposed to enhance the generalisation, transferability, and data efficiency of GNN-based traffic forecasting models. This survey systematically reviews and categorises 42 methods into a unified taxonomy through meta-analysis. We compile a comprehensive list of datasets and open-source implementations, highlighting key challenges and future research directions. This is the first comprehensive review of transfer learning in GNN-based spatiotemporal traffic forecasting. We also provide an actively maintained GitHub repository that tracks the latest papers, codes, and datasets in this domain.

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper examines EU global value-chain (GVC) integration and analyzes its drivers using machine learning models, with case studies of Portugal and Belgium. GVC participation appears to boost productivity and technology upgrading, but also brings concentration risks in the current environment. Results indicate labor cost, labor productivity and human capital as key drivers, supported by infrastructure, manufacturing base, and governance quality. Portugal remains downstream, constrained by low high-tech intensity, while Belgium is highly integrated but exposed to sectoral shocks. Strengthening the EU single market, capital-market integration, and individual countries’ investment in skills, innovation, and diversification would bolster resilience while preserving the benefits of openness.

detail.abstract: This study aimed to identify distinct personality configurations among adult psychotherapy clients using character accentuation profiles obtained in routine clinical practice. A cluster analytic approach was applied to standardized accentuation scores to explore person-centered patterns of personality organization. The analysis revealed three qualitatively distinct personality configurations characterized by different patterns of emotional reactivity, regulation, and interpersonal expression. Importantly, these configurations did not reflect uniform gradations of personality severity but rather distinct modes of personality organization. The findings support a configuration-based perspective on personality assessment in clinical settings and provide a structural foundation for subsequent analyses examining clinical, anamnestic, and mechanistic correlates of personality configurations in psychotherapy clients.

detail.abstract: Energy-efficient lighting is a critical component of sustainable electricity consumption, particularly in developing countries where rising energy demand directly impacts household expenses and national energy planning. This study presents a comprehensive data-driven analysis of electric bulbs available in the Nepalese market using a real-world observational dataset. The dataset includes technical, economic, and user-centric attributes such as wattage, luminous output, energy consumption, color temperature, lifespan, price, and consumer ratings. A detailed exploratory data analysis is conducted to identify consumption trends, efficiency variations, and cost-performance trade-offs among different bulb categories. In addition, a lightweight predictive modeling framework is demonstrated as a proof-of-concept to estimate relative energy consumption under standardized usage assumptions. The results reveal substantial variation in luminous efficiency and long-term cost-effectiveness across brands, indicating that higher price does not always imply better energy performance. This research contributes a localized empirical perspective on lighting efficiency in Nepal and demonstrates how data science methodologies can support evidence-based consumer awareness and policy-level energy efficiency initiatives without requiring complex infrastructure or deployed systems.

The supervisor provided guidance but had no influence over the analysis or conclusions.

detail.abstract: California's Senate Bill 53, enacted in September 2025, establishes the nation's first state-level AI whistleblower protections through Labor Code § § 1107-1107.2. Yet SB 53 perpetuates a structural conflict that creates significant barriers to effective disclosure. Evidence required to substantiate catastrophic AI risk claims (model architectures, training data compositions, safety evaluation results, internal capability assessments) would likely qualify as trade secrets protected under California's Uniform Trade Secrets Act. Labor Code § 1102.5(g) explicitly provides that whistleblower protections do not apply to employer actions against employees who disclose trade secrets, meaning CUTSA-protected information falls outside the statute's shield. The collision creates a legal Catch-22: whistleblowers who make generic claims are dismissed; those who provide specifics face civil damages, criminal prosecution, and exclusion from statutory protection. This paper demonstrates that the conflict is structural rather than incidental, that existing trade secret exceptions are unlikely to resolve it, and that case studies at Google, OpenAI, and Meta confirm the pattern empirically. This paper recommends two reforms: first, a narrow amendment to Civil Code § 3426.1 creating a safe harbor that excludes from "misappropriation" disclosures of reasonably necessary information to designated state bodies for reporting significant AI-related public harm; second, establishing a technically competent recipient body, as neither the Office of Emergency Services nor the Attorney General currently possesses AI safety expertise.

title: Beyond Gold: A Fundamental Valuation of Bitcoin as a Non-Sovereign Asset

detail.title: Beyond Gold: A Fundamental Valuation of Bitcoin as a Non-Sovereign Asset
detail.abstract: The valuation of Bitcoin (BTC) challenges traditional financial metrics, as the asset generates no intrinsic cash flow and lacks sovereign backing. This paper applies a First-Principles Valuation Model based on the discounted future utility of Bitcoin as a non-sovereign Store-of-Value (SoV) commodity. The methodology defines a Composite Total Addressable Market (TAM) of $53.8 trillion, composed of three distinct pools of global capital: Digital Gold, Debt-based Sovereign Reserves, and Offshore Seizure-Resistant Wealth. The model utilizes a Net Present Value (NPV) framework to project the value captured from these pools over a 10-year horizon, discounting the future value (FV) using a risk-adjusted rate (r) reflecting existential uncertainty. A three-tiered scenario analysis (Bull, Base, Bear) yields a broad fundamental value range for the Bitcoin network. The results anchor the value per Bitcoin between the Bear Case of approximately $5,286 and the Bull Case of $66,476, with a Base Case anchor of $16,048. The analysis concludes that the realized value is most sensitive to the successful capture of the Sovereign Reserves pool, an assumption contingent upon the resolution of extreme regulatory and political friction over the next decade.

title: Evidence of Regional Convergence Clubs in Asia
affiliations: University of the Philippines, Asian Development Bank, Asian Development Bank and Asian Development Bank

detail.title: Evidence of Regional Convergence Clubs in Asia
detail.abstract: This paper examines the presence of regional convergence clubs in Asia and identifies relevant factors affecting club membership. Regional cooperation and integration (RCI) from 2003 to 2019 is measured using the Asia-Pacific Regional Cooperation and Integration Index, which is also the key criteria to identify convergence clubs and its members. First, the number of clubs are determined using the Phillips and Sul log-t convergence tests. Second, an ordered probit regression analysis is used to study the determinants of RCI convergence club formation. Our results show that multiple RCI convergence clubs exist in Asia, and that the number of clubs differ across various dimensions of RCI. Initial levels of regional integration, initial levels of extraregional activity and industrial structure are important factors in determining whether a country belongs to a high RCI club or not. However, the magnitude and direction of their impact on club membership is heterogenous across different dimensions.

title: Voter-Directed Democracy Vouchers. A Fiscal, Democratic and Constitutionally Sound Reform of Public Election Funding in Australia

detail.title: Voter-Directed Democracy Vouchers. A Fiscal, Democratic and Constitutionally Sound Reform of Public Election Funding in Australia
detail.abstract: Australia's system of public election funding is built on an automatic entitlement model: political parties and candidates who reach a vote threshold are reimbursed a fixed amount per vote after each election. While intended to reduce reliance on private donations, this mechanism has produced unintended outcomes-reinforcing entrenched parties, rewarding opacity, and guaranteeing public expenditure regardless of voter intent or candidate conduct. This white paper proposes a Voter-Directed Democracy Voucher system to replace the current per-vote reimbursement model. Under this approach, public funding is allocated only when voters actively direct a small, equal-value voucher to candidates who meet strict transparency and independence standards. Public funds are therefore spent by consent, not by default. The proposed model is fiscally conservative, democratically empowering, resistant to corruption, and constitutionally defensible. In all plausible participation scenarios, it results in substantially lower public expenditure than the existing system, while improving electoral fairness and accountability.

title: Climate Resilience and the Adaptation Trap: A Macroeconomic Framework for Joint Fiscal–External Sustainability
affiliations: ISEG Lisbon School of Economics and Management,Universidade de Lisboa, University of Lisbon,  and

detail.title: Climate Resilience and the Adaptation Trap: A Macroeconomic Framework for Joint Fiscal–External Sustainability

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Climate change is reshaping sovereign risk and macroeconomic stability by amplifying fiscal and external fragilities. This paper develops a unified framework to assess how climate vulnerability and resilience jointly influence fiscal–external solvency. We construct a market-based sustainability index that integrates time-varying fiscal and external reaction coefficients – estimated using Schlicht’s (2021) method-weighted by sovereign yields. Using a global panel of more than 60 economies (1981–2024), we document four key findings. First, structural vulnerability exerts a large and persistent drag on sustainability, even after controlling for macro fundamentals, as higher exposure magnifies expected losses and tightens financing conditions. Second, resilience does not display a strong unconditional effect but significantly mitigates the adverse impact of vulnerability, acting as a state-contingent stabilizer. Third, local projections with smooth transition (LP-STAR) reveal sharp nonlinearities: identical climate shocks trigger modest, short-lived effects in low-vulnerability or high-resilience regimes but cause deep and persistent deterioration when vulnerability is high and resilience weak. Fourth, these dynamics generate an “adaptation trap” – a self-reinforcing cycle where vulnerability raises yields, yields compress fiscal space, and limited adaptation perpetuates vulnerability. Policy implications are clear: resilience investment yields sizable macro-financial returns by reducing expected losses and compressing climate risk premia, while delaying adaptation risks entrenching fragility. Our results highlight the need to embed climate parameters into debt sustainability analyses and sovereign risk frameworks, particularly for emerging markets facing tighter financing constraints.

title: India – Thailand Expatriation: Experiences and Dynamics
affiliations: and Suresh Gyan Vihar University Jaipur

detail.title: India – Thailand Expatriation: Experiences and Dynamics
detail.abstract: This study reviews expatriation through an India-Thailand lens, situating contemporary Indian professional mobility within a more extended history of South Asian presence in Thailand. While expatriation has been widely studied within Western and North-South frameworks, far less attention has been paid to South-South mobility and the everyday experiences of Indian professionals and their families in Southeast Asia. Despite the longstanding historical, cultural, and religious ties between India and Thailand, Indian expatriates in Thailand remain an under-researched diaspora, particularly in relation to family life, gendered experiences, social networks, cultural knowledge, and organisational support for expatriates and their families. Drawing on a critical review of forty peer-reviewed studies published between 2014 and 2024, this study synthesises existing research on expatriate motivations, adaptation processes, gender dynamics, and support structures relevant to Indian professionals in Thailand. The review highlights how expatriation outcomes are shaped not only by organisational practices but also by diasporic identity, family well-being, and everyday negotiations of belonging within the host society. By foregrounding South-South mobility and centring the perspectives of Indian expatriates and accompanying family members, this study contributes to South Asian diaspora scholarship and calls for more context-sensitive, gender-aware, and inclusive approaches to understanding expatriation in the Global South.

title: LLM-Augmented Quantitative Finance: A Rigorous Structural Framework for Market State Inference and Forecasting

detail.title: LLM-Augmented Quantitative Finance: A Rigorous Structural Framework for Market State Inference and Forecasting
detail.abstract: Traditional quantitative finance relies on structured numerical data and explicitly specified stochastic dynamics, often failing to incorporate unstructured information such as news, policy language, and market narratives. Large language models (LLMs) can extract semantic representations from text but, when used as end-to-end forecasters, typically lack probabilistic coherence, interpretability, and stability guarantees. This paper proposes a rigorous LLM-augmented framework in which LLMs operate as latent state inference engines rather than direct predictors. Textual information is mapped into a low-dimensional semantic state that conditions regime-switching and state-space dynamics governing returns and volatility. The design preserves probabilistic structure while enabling disciplined incorporation of narrative information unavailable to purely numerical models. We establish formal properties including validity of text-conditioned transition kernels, exact Bayesian filtering recursions, explicit Lipschitz stability with respect to semantic perturbations, and identifiability under a transparent normalization. The framework is suited to leakage-controlled empirical evaluation and reproducible out-of-sample forecasting.

title: Party Pressure and Representation

detail.title: Party Pressure and Representation

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: I study how political parties affect representation in the U.S. House. To do so, I account for party pressure on the votes of members in an otherwise standard spatial model that uses roll call voting patterns to identify member ideologies. I simultaneously estimate voter ideologies from survey responses, leveraging their responses on issues before Congress to bridge voters and members into the same ideological space. I find that, relative to a model without party pressure, member ideologies and those of their constituents are much more closely aligned. The results imply that, in terms of actual votes, parties drive a wedge between members and those they represent. I provide evidence that parties do so strategically, balancing the need for legislative wins and the electoral concerns of their members.

title: Political Ideologies, Redistribution and Local (Mis-)Perceptions of Migrant Stocks and Flows
affiliations: Goettingen University, , Heidelberg University and The University of Western Australia - Department of Economics

detail.title: Political Ideologies, Redistribution and Local (Mis-)Perceptions of Migrant Stocks and Flows

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Do factual immigration updates shift societal concerns across political ideologies? Conducting an online experiment in the lead-up to the 2024 U.S. Presidential Election, respondents provided local immigrant stock and flow estimates before being randomized to receive realistic information on stocks or flows, framed as constant or rising. Most respondents overestimate stocks and flows, with asymmetries emerging across ideologies. Information treatments lower redistribution and tax concerns by 5.4 percentage points on average. Immigration attitudes remain unchanged. Liberals overestimate stocks most, responding to stock treatments. Conservatives overstate flows more, responding to flow information. This pattern is consistent with motivated reasoning: identity-linked immigration views are resistant to correction, while redistribution concerns are elastic to facts when information targets the migration dimension most salient to each ideology.

title: Colonial Extraction and the Drain of Wealth in India

detail.title: Colonial Extraction and the Drain of Wealth in India
detail.abstract: This study examines the mechanisms, magnitude, and consequences of colonial extraction in India under British rule. Drawing upon archival sources, Parliamentary Papers, Reserve Bank of India historical data, the analyses of Dadabhai Naoroji and Utsa Patnaik, and open-source AI-assisted reconstructions, this paper reconstructs the fiscal, trade, and labor-based drains from India to Britain. It emphasizes structural wage denial, informal transfers, deindustrialization, and long-term economic consequences for India. The study applies a quantitative framework defining Total Load (TL) as the sum of documented flows (DF), wage denial (WD), and coercive transfers (CT), and calculates Net Colonial Profit (NP) by subtracting extraction costs (EC). Conservative estimates indicate a Total Colonial Load of approximately £145 trillion (2025 GBP) and a Net Colonial Profit of £142 trillion (2025 GBP). By combining narrative analysis with quantitative reconstruction, the paper provides a detailed understanding of the historical drain of wealth and its structural impact on India's economy.

title: Are Diversified Distribution Channels Increasing Resilience to Climate and Geopolitical Shocks? Evidence From Small Cognac Producers

detail.title: Are Diversified Distribution Channels Increasing Resilience to Climate and Geopolitical Shocks? Evidence From Small Cognac Producers

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Declaration of Interest The author declares no conflicts of interest. This research was conducted independently without financial support from industry organizations, governmental agencies, or private entities. The author has no employment, consulting relationships, stock ownership, honoraria, or other financial interests in organizations related to Cognac production or distribution. Producer anonymization ensures no individual business interests influenced the research design, data collection, analysis, or interpretation of findings.

detail.abstract: Small-scale agricultural producers face mounting pressures from converging climate and geopolitical crises, yet limited research examines how commercial diversification strategies affect producer-level resilience. This paper exploits a natural experiment in France's Cognac region, where producers experienced severe concurrent shocks between 2019 and 2025: spring frosts destroying up to 40% of yields, violent hailstorms, US tariffs of 25%, and Chinese anti-dumping duties reaching 39%. These disruptions affected a sector with 98% export dependency, causing a 22% collapse in export volumes and a projected 37% decline in 2024 production. Using micro-level data from ten independent producers, we construct a novel continuous diversification index capturing the balance across direct sales, négociant contracts, and agritourism channels. We find a strong positive relationship (r ≈ 0.85, p < 0.01) between diversification and operational resilience. Multi-channel producers maintained continuity despite repeated shocks, while mono-channel producers experienced severe financial distress. However, we document a critical "export diversification paradox": producers most heavily engaged in international markets through négociant channels, despite higher overall diversification scores, suffered the most immediate revenue losses from trade tariffs. These findings suggest that diversification strategies must account for underlying risk exposure profiles. For small producers in export-dependent sectors, resilience appears strongest when diversification emphasizes locally-anchored channels less sensitive to international volatility. Results inform agricultural policy design for climate adaptation and trade uncertainty contexts.

title: Digital Data Transparency Act: A Framework for Purpose-Based Disclosure of Data Use

detail.title: Digital Data Transparency Act: A Framework for Purpose-Based Disclosure of Data Use

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Completely unfunded and totally independent

detail.abstract: The Digital Data Transparency Act establishes a statutory framework requiring public disclosure of the functional purposes for which collected data is used or transferred. The Act does not restrict data collection, trade, or analysis. Instead, it ensures that individuals and the public can understand how data contributes to commercial, governmental, and policy-related activities, without requiring disclosure of sensitive methods or operational detail. The Act introduces purpose-based transparency, allowing lawful data use to continue while improving public trust, institutional accountability, and market clarity in an increasingly datadriven economy.

title: Philosophy As Stratigraphy. A Diagnostic Method for Reading History Through Emergent Ideas: Why Ideas Recur, Why Solutions Don't Transfer, And How to Read the Symptoms. A Cross-Disciplinary Framework Integrating Philosophy of History, Evolutionary Psychology, And Institutional Theory

detail.title: Philosophy As Stratigraphy. A Diagnostic Method for Reading History Through Emergent Ideas: Why Ideas Recur, Why Solutions Don't Transfer, And How to Read the Symptoms. A Cross-Disciplinary Framework Integrating Philosophy of History, Evolutionary Psychology, And Institutional Theory

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest. This research was conducted independently and was not commissioned by or produced on behalf of any organization. The author's professional role as a cybersecurity practitioner has no bearing on the historical and philosophical analysis presented in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study involves historical and philosophical analysis of published texts and does not involve human participants, personal data, or primary empirical research requiring ethics approval.

detail.abstract:
The Puzzle. Why do philosophical movements recur across disconnected civilizations? Why does Confucius feel prescriptive today rather than merely historical? Why did the Axial Age produce convergent ideas in China, India, Greece, Persia, and Israel—societies with no contact—between 800 and 200 BCE?

The Claim. This paper proposes a diagnostic inversion: philosophy as symptom, not commentary; systemic pressure as cause, ideas as readout. Like geologists reading sedimentary layers to infer ancient conditions, we can read philosophical emergence to diagnose civilizational stress. We use "stratigraphy" not as a metaphor for passive layering, but as a method of diagnostic inference—where each philosophical formation encodes the conditions of its emergence.

The Method. The framework imports stratigraphic inference rules: index ideas (reliably diagnostic of specific pressures), ideational gaps (where expected responses fail to appear), configuration facies (same pressure producing different local expressions), and cross-civilizational correlation (criteria for treating convergence as evidential). These rules transform pattern-recognition into disciplined diagnosis with explicit falsifiability conditions.

The Mechanism. A three-layer model explains both recurrence and variation: universal biological hardware (evolved psychology, threat-regression dynamics) explains why philosophical problems recur; geographic constraints explain regional variation—why the same pressure produces Confucianism in river-valley China but Stoicism in maritime Rome; cultural software explains specific timing and content. Configuration lock-in—the mutual adaptation of institutions, trust structures, and identity into self-reinforcing systems—explains why solutions fail to transfer across contexts.

The Evidence. Two deep case studies demonstrate the method: fragmentation-response philosophy (Warring States China ↔ Late Roman Republic) and meaning-crisis philosophy (heterodox India ↔ post-WWI Europe). Additional cases are compressed into a diagnostic matrix specifying what should and should not emerge under each pressure type.

The Payoff. The framework generates testable predictions: under fragmentation, order-seeking ethics should increase relative to baseline; under stability, such philosophies should decrease in selection advantage. This offers a mechanistic alternative to cyclical determinism, poetic vagueness ("history rhymes"), and generational theories, providing a diagnostic tool for navigating contemporary crises by understanding which historical medicines might fit which contemporary configurations.

title: Does Growth Shift Relative Prices Against Itself?

detail.title: Does Growth Shift Relative Prices Against Itself?
detail.abstract:
This paper replicates the empirical analysis of Acemoglu and Ventura (2002), which examines whether economic growth endogenously shifts a country’s terms of trade against itself through general equilibrium effects. The original study challenges the conventional view that faster economic growth unambiguously improves a country’s gains from trade, arguing instead that growth-induced changes in global relative prices may offset part of these gains.

Using a cross-country dataset covering the period 1965–1985, this replication estimates the relationship between real GDP per capita growth and terms of trade growth. To address potential endogeneity concerns arising from reverse causality and omitted variables, the analysis employs an instrumental variables approach, using the logarithm of initial GDP per capita as an instrument for subsequent growth. The empirical strategy follows the methodology of the original paper, including Ordinary Least Squares and two-stage least squares estimations, as well as adjustments for structural heterogeneity across countries.

The results confirm the central finding of Acemoglu and Ventura (2002). While ordinary least squares estimates suggest no significant relationship between growth and terms of trade, instrumental variable estimates reveal a statistically significant negative effect of GDP growth on terms of trade growth. This indicates that faster-growing economies tend to experience adverse movements in relative prices, consistent with the general equilibrium feedback mechanism proposed in the original model. Overall, the replication supports the view that economic growth does not automatically translate into improved external price conditions and highlights the importance of accounting for endogeneity in cross-country growth regressions.

title: Coordination Problems in Money Market Funds and Macroprudential Constraints
affiliations: European Securities and Markets Authority , ,  and IÉSEG School of Management, Lille Campus

detail.title: Coordination Problems in Money Market Funds and Macroprudential Constraints

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No declaration of interest

detail.abstract: We develop a game-theoretic model of asset liquidation by money market funds (MMFs) under stressed redemption requests. When each MMF follows ad-hoc liquidation rules such as the proportional liquidation rule, and accounts only for its own constraints, price impact can create excessive resale externalities and, in general, prevent the existence of a Nash equilibrium. We introduce a macroprudential framework in which each MMF internalizes other funds' regulatory constraints (a shared constraint or coupled constraint game) and prove that, under mild conditions, a Nash equilibrium exists and coincides with the social planner's solution that minimizes total illiquid sales subject to feasibility. The result formalizes how macroprudential coordination mitigates price-mediated contagion and highlights policy levers to reduce systemic fragility.

title: Uniform and Participation-expanding Reforms in Decentralized Redistribution: Who Gains and Who Loses?

detail.title: Uniform and Participation-expanding Reforms in Decentralized Redistribution: Who Gains and Who Loses?
detail.abstract: Across many settings, from social transfers to education and health services, reforms that aim to make access uniformly easier for everyone often exacerbate inequality. When access to the redistributive surplus is determined through competition, such reforms increase players' efficiency in the contest but also raise the endogenous efficiency threshold for participation. I formalize this threshold-shifting mechanism in a model of decentralized redistribution, where heterogeneous efficiencies determine both who competes and how the redistributive surplus is allocated. The model delivers two main results. First, a uniform efficiency gain-i.e., equal reductions in access costs-does not expand participation. Instead, it amplifies inequality among participants by reinforcing the relative efficiency of those who were already highly efficient prior to the reform. Yet, such a reform also reduces contest-induced welfare loss, thereby giving rise to an equity-efficiency trade-off. Second, a participation-expanding reform that brings excluded players into the contest can reduce both inequality and welfare loss, particularly when: (i) the new entrants are sufficiently efficient relative to the average participant; and (ii) the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI) of endogenous contest strengths-measuring the extent to which players' efficiencies exceed the participation threshold-is sufficiently high before the reform; for example, when a few strong participants dominate the competition for redistributive surplus.

title: General Theory on Structural Constraints: Investment Traps, Expectation Formation, and the Conditional Nature of Policy Effects

detail.title: General Theory on Structural Constraints: Investment Traps, Expectation Formation, and the Conditional Nature of Policy Effects

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced the research presented in this paper.

detail.abstract:
This paper proposes a structural diagnostic framework in macroeconomics to explain why monetary easing and conventional macroeconomic policies have ceased to generate sustained growth in advanced economies. Rather than interpreting this phenomenon as a failure of policy implementation or as a temporary demand shortfall, the paper conceptualizes it as a transition toward a stage in which investment opportunities themselves become structurally constrained.

The core contribution of the framework is the introduction of the structural frontier coefficient Φ, a theoretical variable representing latent constraints generated by demographic conditions, institutional environments, and capital structures. Φ is not directly observable and is not intended to be precisely measured. Instead, it serves as an ordinal indicator of an economy’s relative position with respect to its capacity to absorb productive investment. Accordingly, this paper does not aim to numerically predict growth rates, inflation, or policy effects, but rather to provide a diagnostic framework that clarifies under which structural conditions existing macroeconomic theories and policy instruments are effective, and under which conditions they are neutralized.

Within this framework, when Φ exceeds a critical threshold θ, standard models such as the Solow growth model and New Keynesian frameworks operate effectively. When Φ falls below θ, however, monetary expansion fails to generate real investment and instead manifests primarily as asset price inflation or capital outflows. This regime is defined as an investment trap, while phenomena such as liquidity traps and secular stagnation are interpreted as approximate manifestations observed within this structurally constrained domain, rather than as fundamental causes.

The paper further hypothesizes that, as economies mature, the elasticity of substitution among structural components declines sharply. Under such conditions, the most binding constraint effectively governs investment feasibility, producing a bottleneck structure. To capture this property, a minimum operator is introduced not as a production or forecasting function, but as a diagnostic approximation to identify the dominant structural constraint.

By rigorously separating structural variables from outcome variables, the framework avoids circular reasoning and offers an identification strategy based on asymmetric responses of investment allocation, employment, growth, and inflation to monetary policy. Time-series and cross-country evidence, including the case of Japan, is shown to be consistent with the central prediction that declining structural frontiers qualitatively neutralize the growth channel of monetary policy.

The contribution of this paper lies not in prescribing specific policies, but in providing a general diagnostic framework that systematically excludes structurally ineffective policy options prior to policy selection.

title: Reducing the Measure of our Ignorance: Useful Exergy's Explanatory Power for TFP and Growth in a normalized CES Supply-Side Approach
affiliations: Goethe University Frankfurt, Instituto Nacional de Investigação Agrária e Veterinária (INIAV, I.P.) - MARETEC and University of Lisbon - Instituto Superior Técnico

detail.title: Reducing the Measure of our Ignorance: Useful Exergy's Explanatory Power for TFP and Growth in a normalized CES Supply-Side Approach

declarations.funderStatement: The work of Julian Salg, Jo˜ao Santos, and Tiago Domingos was supported by FCT/MCTES (PIDDAC) through projects UIDB/50009/2020, UIDP/50009/2020, and LA/P/0083/2020 as well as the MAPS project funded by the European Union’s Horizon Europe Research and Innovation Programme under Grant Agreement Nº 101137914. The authors wish to thank Rainer Klump, Georg D¨urnecker, Matthew Heun, and Vanessa Christiansen for their friendly review as well as participants of International Exergy Economics Conferences and the ESEE Conference 2024 for suggestions and comments to an earlier version of this paper. Julian Salg also thanks “GRADE Sustain” of the Goethe Research Academy for Early Career Researchers (GRADE) for two travel grants. A special thanks goes to Paul Brockway for organizing the International Exergy Economics Conferences, which were the starting point of this research collaboration.

detail.abstract: This study challenges a long-standing critique in ecological economics: that standard neoclassical aggregate production function models systematically underestimate the role of energy in economic growth due to their reliance on the "Cost Share Theorem." According to this theorem, the output elasticity of energy is assumed to equal its relatively small cost share. As a result, conventional models attribute much of economic growth to an unexplained technical residual. We reject this interpretation and introduce the first empirical Constant Elasticity of Substitution (CES) production function that allows for a high output elasticity of energy while still adhering to the Cost Share Theorem. To do this, we use thermodynamically grounded data-specifically, "useful exergy"-as a proxy for the physical energy services actually delivered in production. Our approach is enabled by newly available factor price data for this biophysical input, presented by Santos et al. (2025). These prices reflect the effective costs of energy services and are significantly higher than conventional final energy market prices. Using this data, we consistently treat the biophysical input as an intermediate input to gross output production and align its output elasticity with its average empirical cost share of approximately 30%. Applying the normalized CES supply-side system estimation technique developed by Klump et al. (2007a) to data from the Portuguese economy (1960-2014), we find that: (1) the energy service proxy acts as a complement to capital and labor, with a substitution elasticity below unity; (2) useful exergy internalizes most energy-related technical change, making a separate factor-augmenting technical progress term statistically insignificant; and (3) compared to conventional final energy metrics, useful exergy improves the model's error properties and adds explanatory power by reducing the unexplained portion of value-added growth (i.e., value-added TFP). Ultimately, the combination of quality-adjusted primary factors and our proxy for energy services in the CES model leaves little of Portugal's economic growth unexplained.

title: When Beliefs Become Entrenched: Narrative Dominance and Mispricing in Equity Markets

detail.title: When Beliefs Become Entrenched: Narrative Dominance and Mispricing in Equity Markets
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether narrative dominance contributes to mispricing in equity markets and whether investor sentiment conditions the magnitude of this effect. We focus on periods in which a single market belief becomes entrenched, using sustained growth outperformance as a market-based proxy for the belief that valuation-based investing is obsolete. Using monthly US equity factor data, we find periods of strong narrative dominance are followed by significantly higher future returns to value strategies. These effects emerge in future returns rather than contemporaneous performance, strengthen at longer horizons, and persist after controlling for market volatility, consistent with delayed mispricing correction rather than time-varying risk. We further show the relationship between narrative dominance and subsequent value returns is substantially amplified during periods of elevated investor sentiment. This interaction suggests narrative-driven mispricing is most severe in optimistic environments where arbitrage constraints are more likely to bind. Together, the results highlight the complementary roles of belief content and sentiment in shaping mispricing dynamics and factor return behavior.

title: The Evolution of the Social Contract: Addressing Multi-Culturalism and Minority Representation in a Globalized Era

detail.title: The Evolution of the Social Contract: Addressing Multi-Culturalism and Minority Representation in a Globalized Era
detail.abstract:
Purpose: This paper examines the evolution and contemporary relevance of social contract theory in an era characterized by rapid globalization, fluid demographics, and complex political landscapes. It explores how traditional philosophies—formulated by thinkers such as Thomas Hobbes and John Locke—translate into modern constitutional frameworks and whether these frameworks sufficiently address the needs of a diverse, sectarian society.
Methodology/Approach: The study utilizes a comparative analysis between original social contract theory and modern constitutionalism. It further employs a case study approach, focusing on the political representation of ethnic minorities in Northern Europe, specifically the Swedish Assembly of Finland (Folktinget) and the Sami Parliaments in Finland, Norway, and Sweden.
Findings: The research highlights a significant disconnect between original social contract traditions and modern governance, noting that constitutions are often drafted by committees rather than through the direct collective choice of all citizens. The case study reveals that while specialized institutions like the Sami Parliament provide a platform for indigenous and minority voices, their authority is often limited to consultative and advisory functions. This limitation represents a "delimiting of power" that challenges the social contract’s ideal of equal regulation and political agency for all social groups.
Conclusion: The paper concludes that while social contract theory may not be a singular solution for all political disputes, it offers a vital framework for improving governance flexibility and transparency. The study advocates for an updated set of modern principles that can accommodate diverse factions and expatriate populations to prevent social problems and ensure that basic human rights are applied universally.

title: The TIDE Universe: Tracing a Storytelling-Centred Research Programme in Economics Education

detail.title: The TIDE Universe: Tracing a Storytelling-Centred Research Programme in Economics Education

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve patients or clinical populations. The work draws on classroom-based teaching practice and previously conducted educational studies involving student participants. Participation in all classroom activities and surveys was voluntary, and no personally identifiable information was collected. Written informed consent was obtained from participants where data were used for research purposes. In accordance with institutional practice for non-clinical educational research, formal ethics committee approval was not required.
