detail.abstract: Over several years of teaching and research, a coherent body of work has gradually taken shape around the use of storytelling in economics education. This work spans the design of classroom narratives, conceptual comparison of textbook-based and story-based explanation, systematic attention to student voices, a review of storytelling measurement practices, the development of a diagnostic framework and scale, and a set of empirical studies examining attitudes, recall, perceived utility, and demographic variation. Rather than representing isolated or opportunistic studies, these efforts together constitute a connected research programme, referred to in this article as the TIDE universe. This essay brings that universe together in a single narrative. It explains how the work emerged from classroom practice, how different strands developed in response to unresolved questions, and how the TIDE framework functions as an integrative diagnostic core within a broader programme of inquiry. The article does not present new empirical findings. Its purpose is to make visible the structure, progression, and coherence of the TIDE universe, and to situate it within wider discussions on learning experience, engagement, and measurement in economics education. The work that eventually came to be described as the TIDE universe did not begin as a research agenda. It began, quite simply, with teaching. Stories were introduced into economics classrooms as a way of explaining ideas that students routinely found abstract, distant, or difficult to connect with lived experience. Scarcity, opportunity cost, household decision-making, uncertainty, and trade-offs were explained through situations rather than definitions, through sequences of events rather than lists of assumptions.

title: Addendum: The Element of Space in Human Locomotor Dynamics™ (HLD™)

detail.title: Addendum: The Element of Space in Human Locomotor Dynamics™ (HLD™)
detail.abstract: This addendum formally introduces Space as a distinct element within the Human Locomotor Dynamics™ (HLD™) framework. Space governs presence, distance, orientation, and commitment across absence, operating prior to physical engagement and beyond the moment of contact. Unlike elements that resolve through motion, force, or exchange, Space governs allowance—determining when engagement is possible, how distance converts into authority, and how refusal or absence may constitute dominant action. This document functions as a canonical expansion of the original HLD™ disclosure and does not supersede, revise, or diminish the priority of the founding work. The inclusion of Space resolves functional ambiguities that arise when spacing, visibility, approach, and withdrawal are forced into other elemental domains, thereby preserving structural coherence within the HLD™ resolution system. Authorship is asserted solely over the formal inclusion, definition, and role of Space within the HLD™ framework, without claiming ownership over natural phenomena or physical reality.

title: Dispatches from the Record: Clerk Notes No. 8 — Associational Standing (Who is Allowed to Speak when Many People are Hurt?)

detail.title: Dispatches from the Record: Clerk Notes No. 8 — Associational Standing (Who is Allowed to Speak when Many People are Hurt?)

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests, funding sources, or conflicts of interest related to this work.

detail.abstract:
This note applies the constitutional physiology framework to associational standing doctrine, which governs when an organization may sue on behalf of its members. The familiar three-part test requires: (1) members would otherwise have individual standing, (2) the interests are germane to the organization’s purpose, and (3) neither the claim nor relief requires individual member participation.

The doctrine is not mere procedural etiquette or a loose extension of class actions. It regulates representational routing: whether a proxy (the organization) can reliably transmit harm signals it did not personally experience, without distorting or erasing the original individual signals.

Key insights from the lens:

  • The “germane” requirement ensures the organization is structurally suited to carry the signal cleanly.
  • The no-participation prong protects the court’s ability to perceive the harm without needing direct interrogation of each member.
  • Damages claims often fail while injunctive/declaratory claims survive because individualized relief increases the risk of signal distortion.
  • The doctrine is narrower than class actions: class aggregation follows individual standing, while associational standing authorizes proxy speech itself.

Associational standing polices a boundary between access (letting harmed people be heard) and perception (preserving the court’s ability to understand what actually happened). Too strict, and legitimate harms go unheard; too loose, and the proxy speaks over the people it represents.

The anxiety in the doctrine is signal-integrity protection, not formalism. It holds duality without resolution: organizations enable voice, but only when the conduit remains transparent.

The series traces doctrine through physiological structure, emphasizing perception, routing, proxy fidelity, and boundary behaviors. Previous notes: Nos. 0–7

title: Chambers, a Novel

detail.title: Chambers, a Novel

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests, funding sources, or conflicts of interest related to this work.

detail.abstract:
Chambers is a short literary novel that follows Elisabeth (Lisa for most of the piece), a law clerk, as she encounters a structural isomorphism in constitutional doctrine while working in chambers under Justice Barbara Collins Arnold (BCA), a conservative jurist of unflinching professional integrity.

The story does not unfold through dramatic reversals, ideological clashes, or personal crises. It proceeds as a continuous narrowing of perceptual tolerance: a corroborated harm is acknowledged as real and consequential, yet remains excluded by ordinary procedural design. No one acts in bad faith. Procedure functions correctly. No speeches, revelations, or public reckonings occur.

The emotional thesis is simple and unforgiving: admiration is earned through observed integrity; pity arrives only when admiration is complete. Both emotions land simultaneously—at the moment a professional reflex hesitates, not because of new theory or moral pressure, but because corroborated reality can no longer be routed through the existing boundary without visible cost.

The novel is structured to earn reader implication without instruction, vindication, or catharsis. It withholds resolution, moral summary, ideological triumph, and narrative closure. Readers who finish it are left inside the same unresolved dilemma the characters inhabit: what happens when honesty demands change, but the system has no mechanism to accommodate it?

This work is part of an ongoing exploration of structural inevitability in legal and institutional settings. It applies a physiological lens to doctrine and procedure without explicit theorizing on the page—insights emerge through restraint, timing, silence, and the refusal to simplify difficulty.

title: An Economic Theory of Enforcement and Bribery

detail.title: An Economic Theory of Enforcement and Bribery
detail.abstract: This paper develops an economic theory of enforcement and bribery to analyze the resource allocation trade-off between service provision and internal enforcement. Building on the public good distribution framework used in the context of lobbying by Grossman and Helpman (2001) and the enforcement technology established by Munshi (2025), we construct four distinct models of bribery based on the timing of payments (post-detection versus upfront) and the incentive structure of the enforcer. The analysis reveals that the specific mechanics of the corrupt bargain dictate the policy outcome. Theoretical results show that post-detection bribery with performance-based enforcement (Model 1) yields a conditional allocation, where the direction of resource bias depends on the specific marginal incentives at the equal-distribution benchmark. In contrast, we prove that rent-seeking behavior (Model 2) leads to an unconditional verdict: the government always biases allocation in the favor of the violator to maximize shared surplus. Furthermore, upfront bribery (Models 3 and 4) creates powerful incentives to underfund enforcement; under conditions of high bribe efficacy, the benevolent social planner is rationally compelled to allocate all the resources to the violator.

title: Dispatches from the Record: Clerk Notes No. 4 — Qualified Immunity as Memory Precision Under Uncertainty

detail.title: Dispatches from the Record: Clerk Notes No. 4 — Qualified Immunity as Memory Precision Under Uncertainty

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests, funding sources, or conflicts of interest related to this work.

detail.abstract:
This note applies the constitutional physiology framework to qualified immunity doctrine. Courts shield officials from liability unless the constitutional rule violated was "clearly established" at the time of the conduct with sufficient specificity that a reasonable official would have known it was unlawful.

The doctrine is not about denying harm or moral innocence. It regulates the boundary between retrospective perception and prospective, binding memory. Qualified immunity asks: Was sufficiently precise institutional memory (case law, precedent) already available to guide conduct before the act occurred?

This framing explains—without moral overlay:

  • The demand for specificity (vague precedent cannot guide fast action without freezing the system)
  • Fact-pattern proximity requirements (memory must be usable in real time)
  • Rejection of hindsight (retroactive memory formation violates time discipline)
  • Why appellate courts can acknowledge violations while still granting immunity (perception is allowed; new binding memory is not)
  • The upstream role of training, policies, and guidance (they pre-encode memory, reducing cases where immunity must be invoked)

The doctrine protects legitimacy by preventing hindsight contamination and retroactive standard-setting. It holds duality: a constitutional violation may have occurred, yet liability remains barred. This is not incoherence; it is structural time discipline at a boundary.

Professionalism and clear institutional guidance emerge as system-level prevention mechanisms—reducing the need for the doctrine altogether.

The series traces doctrine through physiological structure, focusing on institutional capacity, perceptual limits, memory, and boundary behaviors. Previous notes: Nos. 0–3 (links to be added once live).

detail.abstract: This paper presents the Theory of Post-Sectoral Value-Labour Decoupling, in which the classical three sectors of the economy (agriculture, industry, and services) lose their ability to organize and describe urban space. Building on the classical Three Sectors Theory formulated by Fourastier, Fischer, and Clark, the author shows how automation of work and the growth of value generated by digitalization lead to the phenomenon termed detertialization: the decline of employment in the service sector alongside the increase of digital and algorithmic income. This results in a decoupling of work and economic value and the emergence of a post-sectoral economy. The theory integrates Lefebvre's analysis of the production of space, demonstrating that the city ceases to be an object of sectoral functions and becomes a co-planning subject acting in real time. Social and economic indicators for each sector are introduced, along with a Sectoral E iciency Index to measure the relationship between economic value and employment. The theory is conceptual but grounded in observable trends: automation, digitalization, and the development of data infrastructure. This framework o ers a tool for urban studies, economics, and sociology to analyze cities in the algorithmic era.

title: Dispatches from the Record Clerk Notes No. 1 -Standing, or: When Seeing Is Not Acting

detail.title: Dispatches from the Record Clerk Notes No. 1 -Standing, or: When Seeing Is Not Acting

detail.abstract:
This note applies a constitutional physiology framework to standing doctrine. Courts act as the civic system's perceptual organ, receiving and interpreting harm signals (evidence of injury). However, perception does not automatically trigger action—standing enforces a structural boundary between judicial recognition of harm and institutional command.

The familiar elements align under this lens:

  • Injury in fact localizes actionable harm signals.
  • Causation ensures traceability without distortion.
  • Redressability confirms competence to engage the correct mechanism.

Generalized grievances are perceivable but not locally actionable, so judicial perception lacks legitimate routing to act.

This view reframes standing not as gatekeeping or evasion, but as boundary enforcement: it preserves duality between acknowledgment (recognition, explanation) and command (action, remedy). Dismissals become institutional honesty about limits, not denial of harm.

When standing is absent, courts can still describe harm, explain limits, preserve records, and signal alternative channels—respecting the boundary while allowing indirect care.

The framing explains why opinions feel humane yet firm, protecting legitimacy through restraint. It reveals standing as the doctrine marking the line between seeing and acting, without importing new values.

The series explores legal doctrine through this physiological lens, focusing on institutional capacity and structural constraints. Previous note: Clerk Notes No. 0 (link to be added once live).

This keeps the voice authentic, highlights the "click" moment, and drives downloads to the PDF for the full narrative. It also includes a subtle series reference for continuity.

title: Dispatches from the Record: Clerk Notes No. 7 — Class Actions

detail.title: Dispatches from the Record: Clerk Notes No. 7 — Class Actions

detail.abstract:
This note applies the constitutional physiology framework to class action doctrine under Rule 23. Class actions arise when individual litigation fails to make harm legible: injuries too small, too repetitive, too diffuse, or too structurally identical to process one-by-one.

Certification requires:

  • Numerosity (individual routing impractical)
  • Commonality (shared questions of law or fact)
  • Typicality (representative injury tracks the group)
  • Adequacy (representation does not distort or erase interests)

The doctrine is not about generosity or collectivism. It is perceptual compression: the judiciary temporarily treats many individuals as a single functional unit for perception and action, while preserving individual identity downstream.

This framing explains:

  • Aggressive policing of commonality (prevents distortion of distinct harms)
  • Existential importance of adequacy (ensures signal fidelity)
  • Unease with overbroad classes (risk of erasing individual boundaries)
  • Different treatment of injunctive vs. damages classes (damages demand more individual fidelity)
  • Opt-out rights as structural protection of identity

Class actions hold duality: too much individuality hides patterns in noise; too much collectivity dissolves identity. The system borrows aggregation to see without becoming collective.

Upstream pattern recognition through aggregation expands perception without expanding power.

The series traces doctrine through physiological structure, emphasizing perception, aggregation, signal routing, and boundary behaviors. Previous notes: Nos. 0–6.

title: Dynamic impacts of uncertainties and market panic on green bond market volatility: Fresh evidence from the MRS-GARCH-MIDAS-VIX-Skewed-T model

detail.title: Dynamic impacts of uncertainties and market panic on green bond market volatility: Fresh evidence from the MRS-GARCH-MIDAS-VIX-Skewed-T model
detail.abstract: As a key financial instrument for supporting the global low-carbon transition, the green bond market has its volatility influenced by the interaction of multiple factors. To accurately characterize the volatility features of green bonds, this study undertakes three core tasks: first, constructing the MRS-GARCH-MIDAS-VIX-Skewed-T model, incorporating multi-source uncertainties (Climate Policy Uncertainty (CPU), Global Economic Policy Uncertainty (GEPU), Geopolitical Risk (GPR)) and the CBOE Volatility Index (VIX), and establishing a three-tier analytical framework of ‘long-term uncertainty→short-term market panic→extreme risk distribution’ to provide a more precise quantitative tool for green bond volatility research; second, verifying the state-dependent impact of multi-source uncertainties and VIX on green bond volatility, and clarifying the dynamic changes in the impact intensity of various shocks and market panic with the market’s low/high uncertainty states; third, refining the heterogeneous impacts of multi-source uncertainties and VIX, and distinguishing the functional differences between ‘long-term policy shocks’ and ‘short-term market panic shocks’. Empirical results show that the MRS-GARCH-MIDAS-VIX-Skewed-T model exhibits better fitting and predictive performance, and VIX exerts a significant positive driving effect on the short-term volatility of green bonds; multi-source uncertainties have significant state heterogeneity in their impact on green bond volatility, and the mechanisms of different uncertainty factors and the moderating effect of VIX show heterogeneous characteristics.

title: Dispatches from the Record: Clerk Notes No. 5 — Deliberate Indifference

detail.title: Dispatches from the Record: Clerk Notes No. 5 — Deliberate Indifference

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests, funding sources, or conflicts of interest related to this work.

detail.abstract:
This note applies the constitutional physiology framework to deliberate indifference doctrine, most commonly seen in custodial contexts (prisons, detention, schools, foster care). The standard requires: (1) actual knowledge of a substantial risk of serious harm, and (2) failure to take reasonable measures to address it.

Deliberate indifference is not about intent to harm or negligence. It regulates post-perception signal handling: once a verified harm signal enters the system and is registered, non-response becomes an affirmative institutional choice.

Key insights from the lens:

  • Negligence occurs before perception (missed signals); deliberate indifference occurs after (alarm rang, no reflex routed).
  • Inaction is treated as action because, after awareness, silence is suppression of response.
  • The doctrine clusters in custodial settings because the state controls routing paths and individuals cannot self-rescue, raising responsibility after knowledge.
  • Courts police signal handling, not perfect outcomes—preserving legitimacy by avoiding impossible standards or hindsight governance.

This framing explains why actual knowledge is required, why "doing nothing" is culpable, and why the doctrine feels precise rather than punitive. It holds duality: institutions cannot respond to every risk, but they cannot ignore known, serious harm once perceived.

Upstream training and routing improvements reduce invocations—not by softening standards, but by preventing the conditions that trigger the doctrine.

The series traces doctrine through physiological structure, emphasizing capacity, perception, signal routing, and boundary behaviors. Previous notes: Nos. 0–4.

title: Dispatches from the Record: Clerk Notes No. 6 — Use of Force as High-Risk Reflex Under Uncertainty

detail.title: Dispatches from the Record: Clerk Notes No. 6 — Use of Force as High-Risk Reflex Under Uncertainty

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests, funding sources, or conflicts of interest related to this work.

detail.abstract:
This note applies the constitutional physiology framework to Fourth Amendment use-of-force doctrine (Graham v. Connor and progeny). Courts evaluate whether force was objectively reasonable based on the facts and circumstances confronting the officer at the time—severity of the crime, immediate threat, active resistance or flight—excluding intent, hindsight, and moral judgments untethered from the moment.

The doctrine audits a high-risk motor reflex: fast, dangerous, non-deliberative protective action to prevent imminent harm. The judiciary (perception and interpretation) cannot run the reflex in real time; it can only assess whether the reflex fired within permissible boundaries under uncertainty.

Key alignments:

  • Exclusion of intent and hindsight protects the boundary between perception and reflex—cortical judgment cannot safely govern motor response instantaneously.
  • Objective reasonableness is structural permission for reflex error, not endorsement of outcomes.
  • The standard pairs tightly with qualified immunity: both preserve system capacity to allow necessary force without paralysis.
  • Training and upstream boundary-shaping (recognizing structural inevitability early) reduce reflex invocations more effectively than litigation.

This explains why these cases often feel unsatisfying: courts acknowledge real harm while upholding authorization for reflex. The tension is not failure—it is the cost of permitting high-risk action under uncertainty.

The doctrine holds duality: authorization without endorsement, restraint without paralysis, accountability without mind-reading.

The series traces doctrine through physiological structure, focusing on reflex, perception, capacity, and boundary behaviors. Previous notes: Nos. 0–5.

title: Tacit Collusion and Environmental Externalities in Electricity Markets
affiliations: Italian Regulatory Authority for Energy, Networks and Environment (ARERA) and Università Cattolica del Sacro Cuore

detail.title: Tacit Collusion and Environmental Externalities in Electricity Markets
detail.abstract: We study a duopoly in which electricity producers repeatedly compete in quantities while generating pollution. Firms differ in production costs and per-unit emissions, reflecting technological asymmetries such as those observed in power plants. We examine the conditions under which tacit collusion can be sustained and study welfare-maximizing policies. We show that, if coordinated intervention by an antitrust authority (ensuring competition) and a government (imposing a Pigouvian tax) is not feasible, unilateral intervention by either authority may fail to achieve the optimal outcome. When pollution externalities are sufficiently large, antitrust enforcement may reduce welfare by disrupting collusion that limits emissions through output restraint. Similarly, a Pigouvian tax may fail to prevent collusion. We derive the optimal pollution tax under antitrust enforcement, and we propose second-best tax rates based on firms’ relative production and emission efficiencies when antitrust is (temporarily) ineffective. We discuss such policies, or the lack thereof, in the context of the 2022 energy crisis. Finally, we show that, under the current conditions, the phase-out of the dirtier technology must be accompanied by tight market oversight ensuring competition, else it may reduce welfare.

detail.abstract: This study investigates the relationship between Gross Domestic Product (GDP) and Gross Fixed Capital Formation (GFCF) in Bangladesh and Malaysia over the period 2012-2022. Using data from the World Bank's World Development Indicators and a log-linear Cobb-Douglas production function, the paper estimates the elasticity of output with respect to capital. Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) results indicate a strong and statistically significant positive relationship, with an estimated elasticity of approximately 0.88. While the model explains a large proportion of variation in GDP, diagnostic tests reveal the presence of heteroskedasticity and nonnormal residuals. The findings suggest diminishing returns to capital and highlight the importance of complementary growth strategies.

detail.abstract: Structural transformation in advanced economies is commonly described through sectoral shifts from industrial to service-based employment. This paper argues that such an interpretation overlooks a fundamental spatial consequence of tertiarization: the transformation of location factors themselves. The paper proposes a conceptual shift from labor-based industrial location theory toward an understanding of cognitive location factors, in which knowledge-intensive work, social infrastructure, and urban quality become decisive for spatial competitiveness. Drawing on urban theory and socioeconomic transformation, the paper demonstrates how the rise of cognitive labor reshapes spatial preferences, settlement patterns, and the functional logic of cities. By framing tertiarization as a socio-spatial process rather than a purely economic one, the paper contributes a theoretical model for understanding post-industrial urban reconfiguration and its implications for urban planning and regional development.

title: Multimodal Talent Discovery in Children Using Calibrated Baselines

detail.title: Multimodal Talent Discovery in Children Using Calibrated Baselines

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study analyzes fully anonymized data in compliance with GDPR Article 89(1) for scientific research purposes. All children's works data was collected with explicit parental consent through the talents.kids educational platform. Personal identifiers (names, photographs, contact information, IP addresses) were permanently removed prior to analysis. The dataset contains only anonymized vector data of creative artifacts (drawings, writings, musical compositions, videos) and derived analytical features. No ethics committee approval was required for this retrospective analysis of anonymized educational data under GDPR provisions. Formal ethics committee approval is being pursued from the Portuguese Data Protection Authority (CNPD) for future prospective studies.

detail.abstract: Early identification of children's talents remains a critical challenge in personalized education, traditionally requiring costly expert assessments with limited scalability. We present a multimodal AI system analyzing authentic creative artifacts (drawings, writings, musical compositions, videos) from 5,237 analyses across 479 children to predict talent profiles across 7 domains. Our calibrated classical baselines achieve exceptional performance: Logistic Regression (ROC-AUC 0.9956, F1-macro 0.9734), LightGBM (ROC-AUC 0.9999, F1-macro 0.9972, ECE 0.0018 post-calibration). Temporal validation on 127 children with 3+ longitudinal sessions demonstrates sustained predictive validity (F1-macro 0.833 at 5.7 months, 0.742 at 11.4 months). Multi-agent LLM architecture employing 34 models from 9 providers validates individual model accuracy (Gemini: r>0.98 correlation with meta-model ground truth) while maintaining production cost-efficiency ($0.002–$0.091 per prediction). SHAP interpretability analysis reveals pedagogically aligned feature patterns. Bootstrap confidence intervals (10,000 iterations) quantify prediction uncertainty. This work demonstrates that rigorous calibration and transparent uncertainty quantification enable trustworthy AI deployment in high-stakes educational contexts, with open benchmark and code at github.com/talents-kids promoting reproducible research in educational AI.

title: Deindustrialization as a Functional-Spatial Process: An Urban Theory Perspective

declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Deindustrialization is commonly understood as a sectoral phenomenon reflected in declining industrial employment and the growth of the service sector. This paper argues that such an understanding is insu icient from an urban and spatial planning perspective. Deindustrialization should instead be conceptualized as a functionalspatial process resulting from the loss of adequacy between industrial functions and their established locations. Building on classical theories of industrial location, innovation cycles, and sectoral transformation, this paper proposes a dynamic model of location based on evolving causal location factors (CLFs). It demonstrates that industrial locations follow a life cycle in which technological innovation, economic globalization and glocalization, and social tertiarization progressively undermine the functional suitability of existing spatial structures. The paper introduces an anticipatory planning paradigm that treats deindustrialization not as a disruptive collapse but as a predictable phase of urban transformation. By reframing deindustrialization as a spatial process rather than a sectoral decline, the paper contributes a conceptual framework applicable to metropolitan regions facing post-industrial transition.

detail.abstract:
Hi. I’m glad you’re here.

I’m writing these notes because I’ve discovered a way of learning law that I can’t unsee—and it’s been unexpectedly joyful. Treating the civic system as a literal body, rather than a handy metaphor, has made doctrine feel more precise, more constrained, and more alive than anything I’ve encountered before. I want to see how far this way of learning can take me.

If you’ve spent time clerking, litigating, or working close to courts, you may recognize the instinct that led me here. Law isn’t just argument. It’s structure. It’s timing. It’s constraint. It’s the discipline of working inside a system that cannot see everything, cannot fix everything, and still has to decide.

These notes are for people who enjoy that discipline.

They’re written for those who have felt the quiet satisfaction of watching doctrine behave consistently under pressure. For people who have noticed that some rules endure not because they’re elegant, but because they’re necessary. For anyone curious about how law actually operates once it is placed inside a real institutional body.

One thing I want to say plainly at the outset: this series is not about pedigree. I don’t care how you got here, where you trained, or what you plan to do next. All of that fades once the role begins. What matters is the craft—how the system works, and how you learn to work inside it.

That’s where my interest is.

title: Industrial Clusters at the Threshold of Transformation: The Neckar Valley as an Urban Laboratory for Post-Industrial Change

detail.abstract: Industrial clusters have long been perceived as stable engines of regional development. Yet many of these clusters are currently undergoing profound structural transformations that challenge their spatial foundations. This paper examines the Neckar Valley in the Stuttgart metropolitan region as an urban laboratory for analyzing post-industrial transformation processes. Rather than presenting a descriptive regional study, the paper uses the Neckar Valley as an empirical model to demonstrate how industrial clusters enter a phase of declining functional adequacy between production systems and inherited spatial structures. The analysis integrates technological innovation, global economic restructuring, and sociospatial transformation into a unified explanatory framework. The paper argues that industrial clusters do not dissolve suddenly but transition through identifiable phases that can be anticipated through spatial indicators. By interpreting the Neckar Valley as a transferable analytical model, the study contributes to a broader understanding of post-industrial urban transformation beyond the specific regional context.

title: The Locomotor Dynamics Doctrine (Canonical Resolution Equation)

detail.title: The Locomotor Dynamics Doctrine (Canonical Resolution Equation)
detail.abstract: The Locomotor Dynamics Doctrine formalizes a closed, non-physical framework for resolving opposed human movement through positional authority under constraint. It defines resolution as an emergent outcome of enforceable position rather than force, speed, or reaction, providing a canonical equation that governs how authority is established, constrained, transferred, and finalized between responsive agents. The doctrine specifies lawful transitions, exclusions, and failure states within a fixed interpretive system intended for instructional, analytical, and comparative use.

title: A Sectoral Efficiency Indicator Based on Social and Economic Structural Ratios

detail.title: A Sectoral Efficiency Indicator Based on Social and Economic Structural Ratios

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.

detail.abstract: The classical theory of the three economic sectors, as formulated by Jean Fourastié, conceptualizes structural transformation primarily through shifts in employment between the agrarian, industrial, and service sectors. While this approach provides a robust sociostructural interpretation of development, it remains limited to the social dimension of labor allocation. This paper proposes a complementary methodological extension by introducing an economic sectoral ratio based on sectoral contributions to gross domestic product (GDP) and by relating this economic ratio to the traditional social (employment-based) ratio. The resulting indicator-defined as the quotient of economic and social sectoral ratios-captures sectoral efficiency as a measure of structural productivity. The indicator enables comparative analysis of sectors not only in terms of their relative size but also in terms of their economic utilization of labor. The paper formalizes the indicator, discusses its theoretical foundations, and outlines its analytical potential for economic and structural studies.

detail.abstract: Urban planning in post-industrial regions has largely developed as a reactive practice focused on redevelopment, regeneration, and crisis management. This paper argues that such an approach addresses the symptoms of structural transformation rather than its underlying logic. Post-industrial change is not an exceptional disruption but a predictable phase of socioeconomic and spatial evolution. The paper introduces anticipatory urban planning as a paradigm capable of responding to structural transformation before functional breakdown occurs. Drawing on urban theory, location dynamics, and long-term structural analysis, it conceptualizes planning as a system of foresight, adaptation, and spatial resilience. By reframing planning from regulation of land use to governance of transformation processes, the paper contributes a theoretical foundation for proactive urban strategies in post-industrial regions.

title: Seeing Through Green: Text-Based Classification and the Firm's Returns from Green Patents

detail.title: Seeing Through Green: Text-Based Classification and the Firm's Returns from Green Patents

declarations.funderStatement: Authors claim funding from the European Union - NEXT-GENERATION EU, as part of the project "Fostering Open Science in Social Science Research (FOSSR)" - MUR Code PNRR-IR0000008 - CUP B83C22003950001

detail.abstract: This paper introduces a Natural Language Processing (NLP) approach to identify 'true' green patents from official supporting documents. We start by training a simple neural network on about 12.4 million patents previously classified as green in the literature.The model expands an initial dictionary of environmental technologies through vector representations of semantically related expressions. After testing, we find that 'true' green patents account for about 18.5% of all patents classified as green by conventional methods. We document substantial heterogeneity across technological classes and show that "true" green patents are, on average, about 4% less cited by subsequent inventions. In the second part of the paper, we test the relationship between patenting and a dashboard of firm-level financial accounts in the European Union. After controlling for reverse causality, we show that holding at least one 'true' green patent raises sales, market shares, and productivity. If we restrict the analysis to high-novelty 'true' green patents, we find that they also yield higher profits. Overall, our findings highlight the value of NLP-based text analysis for developing more fine-grained patent classifications, providing useful insights for policymakers and innovation scholars alike.

title: Decentralization, Administrative Geography, and Technology Diffusion in Maoist China

detail.title: Decentralization, Administrative Geography, and Technology Diffusion in Maoist China

declarations.funderStatement: Project supported by the Young Scientists Fund of the National Natural Science Foundation of China (Grant No. 72203187).

detail.abstract: China's decentralized M-form hierarchy granted provincial governments substantial autonomy over economic administration. This paper examines how this territorially organized system shaped the diffusion of agricultural innovation during the Maoist period. Focusing on the spread of high-yield rice varieties in the 1960s and 1970s, it shows that diffusion was strongly mediated by provincial authority: research priorities and extension efforts were organized around province-level assessments of aggregate environmental suitability, producing sharp delays at provincial borders. Within provinces, counties whose environmental conditions diverged from provincial averages benefited less from local suitability in the introduction of semi-dwarf rice. Environmentally marginal counties were disadvantaged both because research and extension systems prioritized dominant provincial environments and because institutional frictions raised the cost of accessing technologies developed elsewhere. Overall, the findings highlight a fundamental trade-off in China's M--form hierarchy between effective intra-provincial coordination and spatial distortions arising from administrative--environmental mismatch.

title: Beyond the Flood: Architectural Vulnerability, Community Resilience, and Governance Lessons from the 2013 Uttarakhand Himalayan Disaster

detail.title: Beyond the Flood: Architectural Vulnerability, Community Resilience, and Governance Lessons from the 2013 Uttarakhand Himalayan Disaster
detail.abstract: The 2013 Uttarakhand disaster represents one of India's most severe climate-induced humanitarian crises, exposing the fragile relationship between Himalayan ecology, built form, and governance systems. Triggered by extreme cloudburst rainfall and amplified by geomorphological instability, the disaster caused extensive loss of life, infrastructure collapse, and long-term socioeconomic disruption. This paper examines the event through an architectural and disaster management lens, focusing on failures in hill-area construction, planning practices, and governance frameworks, while also highlighting the critical role of community response and post-disaster resilience initiatives. Drawing upon verified government reports, international agency assessments, and statutory building codes, the study argues that the magnitude of destruction was not solely the result of natural forces but was significantly intensified by unregulated development and risk-insensitive architectural practices.

detail.abstract: This study measures the economic impact of hotels and similar establishments on the overall economy of the Hungarian Veszprém District. publicationDetails.journalName: BAFFI Centre on Economics, Finance & Regulation Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We study forward-looking climate policy uncertainty through a macro-finance lens, focusing on the transmission of climate uncertainty shocks to aggregate and sectoral dynamics. Using monthly U.S. data from 2014 to 2025, we estimate a Bayesian Proxy-SVAR identified with an external instrument derived from the realized volatility of the ICE U.S. Carbon Futures Index, a market directly exposed to climate regulation. This proxy isolates the unexpected and forward-looking component of climate-policy uncertainty. We find that climate uncertainty shocks tighten financial conditions, raise market volatility and financial stress, and reduce output, prices, and stock market valuations, triggering an accommodative monetary policy response. At the sectoral level, we document heterogeneity along two complementary dimensions. A broad green-brown decomposition shows that transition riskexposed (brown) sectors experience deeper and more persistent contractions, whereas less exposed (green) sectors recover faster. We then perform a full sector-by-sector disaggregation of industrial production and valuation responses and match each sector to its EPA supply-chain emission intensity. This granular mapping reveals a systematic relationship between carbon intensity and the severity of climate uncertainty-induced contractions: higheremission industries exhibit larger and more persistent real and financial declines. Overall, forward-looking climate-policy uncertainty acts as a financial amplifier, propagating primarily through volatility and valuation channels and reinforcing the asymmetric dynamics of the low-carbon transition.

publicationDetails.journalName: Research Institute of Industrial Economics (IFN) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: I study the digital market for attention in a freemium mobile game where users choose between paying with money or by watching 30-second video ads. Using unique event-level data, I estimate consumers' supply elasticity of attention. In the aggregate, a one percent higher price increases the share of users watching videos as a payment by 2.2 percent. A substantial part is due to individual heterogeneity in tastes. When accounting for individual heterogeneity, the elasticity reduces to 0.5. The individual elasticities vary throughout the day, peaking in the evening. Complementing the unique data on each play made by users, I use data on the revenue to the gaming company from showing ads. The data is on an individual and daily level, allowing me to match the individual supply elasticity with the revenue from showing ads to the same individual. I find advertisers pay more to show ads to individuals who are less likely to use ads as their payment method. The effect is stronger among Android users than iOS users.

title: The Importance of Considering Regimes in Long-term Asset Allocation to Real Estate

detail.title: The Importance of Considering Regimes in Long-term Asset Allocation to Real Estate

publicationDetails.journalName: BAFFI Centre on Economics, Finance & Regulation Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We investigate the long-term, regime-dependent asset allocation of an investor's wealth in a mixed-asset portfolio that includes publicly traded real estate. We show that augmenting standard VAR models with Markov-switching features not only improves predictive power for asset returns but also introduces economically meaningful horizon effects in optimal portfolio allocations. As the investment horizon lengthens, optimal portfolio allocations become less sensitive to the prevailing regime. Across initial states, the sensitivity of portfolio allocations to the investment horizon manifests primarily through a gradual reallocation toward risky assets relative to risk-free assets, particularly at lower levels of risk aversion. Public real estate receives economically meaningful portfolio allocations under these conditions. Out-of-sample portfolio tests further show that regime-switching models deliver higher realized utility and Sharpe ratios than linear and i.i.d. benchmarks. Overall, the results highlight the economic value of incorporating regime shifts into longterm portfolio choice and confirm the continued role of publicly traded real estate in mixedasset portfolios.

detail.abstract: This paper analyzes how a reform increasing statutory retirement age from 60 to 64 affected women's incentives for early retirement. In Italy, women can anticipate retirement at 57 (with 35 contribution years), but subject to an annuity penalization. Using Italian administrative data, we compare women eligible for the early retirement scheme before and after the reform, finding a small effect on women's retirement age, but a substantial negative effect on annuity. Effects are stronger for women with low labor market attachment or working full-time, suggesting that reconciliation of paid and unpaid works is an important driver of early retirement choices.

title: The Sovereign Resilience Derivative (SRD): A Financial Engineering Framework for Converting Climate Finance into Perpetual National Wealth

detail.title: The Sovereign Resilience Derivative (SRD): A Financial Engineering Framework for Converting Climate Finance into Perpetual National Wealth
detail.abstract: This paper presents the Sovereign Resilience Derivative (SRD), a financial innovation that converts international climate finance into perpetual, self-sustaining national wealth through a closed-loop mechanism. Unlike traditional aid models that create dependency, or debt financing that creates fragility, the SRD transforms one-time capital injections into permanent wealth-generating systems. The mechanism operates through four phases: sovereign guarantee, bond issuance, sovereign wealth fund creation, and tandem fund investment. By capturing the differential between expensive imported energy and cheap renewable generation, then investing those savings in globally diversified portfolios, developing nations can achieve economic sovereignty within a single generation. The paper demonstrates how this framework embodies the Law of Symbiotic Resilience, creating mutual benefit between guarantor and recipient nations while addressing both climate adaptation and sustainable development goals.

detail.title: Dams and Rural Conflict: Evidence from Brazil's Hydropower Expansion

publicationDetails.journalName: FEEM Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: We estimate the impact of infrastructure investment on conflict using 163 hydroelectric dams in Brazil (2002-2022). Leveraging the staggered rollout of construction in a difference-indifferences framework, we find that dams trigger sharp, temporary surges in land invasions, water disputes, and homicides. These effects peak during construction and dissipate upon operation, suggesting they stem from the displacement process rather than the public good itself. Crucially, conflict is mediated by local institutions: violence occurs only where property rights are weak and displacement affects vulnerable smallholders. Our results demonstrate that without effective compensation, state-led modernization generates destabilizing redistributive shocks.

detail.title: Telework and Local Tax Performance: Work-from-home and What, How, and Where We Consume
detail.abstract: This paper studies the fiscal consequences of fully remote and hybrid work-from-home (WFH) arrangements for subnational governments by examining how they alter the composition and modality of consumption. Using granular administrative tax return data from Tennessee, we analyze how WFH alters the composition of taxable consumption across many types of goods, vendors, local jurisdictions, and property classifications. Exploiting variation in telework potential across counties in a difference-indifferences design, we find that WFH erodes the sales tax base. Declines are concentrated in non-food purchases, lower-value transactions, general merchandise stores, and vendors located in more populous jurisdictions. These patterns are consistent with WFH shifting consumption away from taxable goods and restaurant meals toward largely untaxed services, while also reallocating sales tax revenue from larger to smaller jurisdictions through changes in shopping modality. In contrast, we find only modest effects of WFH on property tax revenues, reflecting limited adjustments in assessments of housing consumption across property types and jurisdictions.

title: The Sovereign Resilience Derivative and the Path to Type 1 Civilization: Applying the Law of Symbiotic Resilience to Achieve Planetary Civilizational Advancement

detail.title: The Sovereign Resilience Derivative and the Path to Type 1 Civilization: Applying the Law of Symbiotic Resilience to Achieve Planetary Civilizational Advancement
detail.abstract: This paper demonstrates how the Sovereign Resilience Derivative (SRD)-the first deliberate engineering application of the Law of Symbiotic Resilience-provides a practical pathway for humanity's transition to a Type 1 civilization on the Kardashev scale. We argue that the SRD's closed-loop financial mechanism addresses the four critical requirements for Type 1 status: planetary energy mastery, economic stability, societal cohesion, and technological integration. By converting linear, extractive economic models into circular, symbiotic systems, the SRD creates the material foundation for unified planetary civilization. The paper presents a phased implementation pathway from local pilots to global deployment, with projections for energy capture, economic growth, and civilizational advancement.

title: Cell Phone Use, Academic Performance, and Social Connections: Evidence from the Exogenous Shock of a Cell Phone Ban

detail.title: Cell Phone Use, Academic Performance, and Social Connections: Evidence from the Exogenous Shock of a Cell Phone Ban
detail.abstract:
Cell phone use and social media apps have a profound impact on students. The Augusta-Richmond County, Georgia school district implemented a cell phone ban at school, starting in Fall 2024. Seizing this opportunity of a quasi-exogenous shock on cell phone use on campus, I conducted a survey of cell phone use, including screen time, number of pick-ups, popular apps, and perceived impact on class performance and campus life, on students in 11th grade (Class of 2026) and 10th grade (Class of 2027) in Spring 2025. I also obtained data collected in Spring 2024 by the school for then-10th grade (Class of 2026).

Screen time for students from Class of 2026 does not go down from the first survey before the cell phone ban to the survey after the ban. The new 10th grade students also do not report statistically significant lower screen time after the ban. The number of pickups for both groups of students is lower after the ban, compared to that for the then 10th grade students (Class of 2026) before the ban. As to the measures of the impacts of the cell phone ban, including classroom engagement, turning in homework on time (homework timeliness), grades, and peer engagement, teachers who participated in the survey after the ban report positive outcomes. Both groups of students report neutral or slightly negative assessments on the improvements of those measures from pre- to post-ban. The differences between teachers and students on these measures are highly statistically significant. Regression analysis using individual level student data from the survey after the ban, however, shows that students with more phone use (higher screen time and greater number of pickup) tend to report more positive improvements in classroom engagement and homework timeliness. Overall, the evidence suggests that the cell phone ban is somewhat effective, but the outcome is not overwhelmingly positive based on student responses.

title: Extended Solow Model with Human Capital and Technology Innovation for Sustainable Economic Growth: The Case of a Logistics Company

detail.title: Extended Solow Model with Human Capital and Technology Innovation for Sustainable Economic Growth: The Case of a Logistics Company
detail.abstract: The central argument in classical growth theory-most pointedly the Solow model-is that growth entirely reliant on labor and physical capital yields diminishing returns, so cannot be maintained long-term. Consequently, economists have paid increasing attention to growth-producing sources in a variety of other areas-particularly such as accumulation of human capital and technological innovation. Using the extended Solow framework, this study also investigates the relationship between human capital, technological innovation, and economic growth and what it means for sustainable development. With Thailand as a case study, the empirical analysis involves the use of ordinary least squares (OLS) regressions to investigate the relationship between education-related indicators as well as R&D expenditure with GDP. Human capital and technological innovation are found to be positively related to economic growth. Secondary enrollment in secondary education and investment in R&D show statistically significant positive associations with GDP, indicating the relationship of productivity with quality of labor and innovation-led productivity. Apart from the empirical evidence, the present paper also covers these growth factors with an eye to sustainable development. Emphasizing the logistics sector, the research demonstrates that investment in education and technology can underpin sustainable economic growth through increased resource efficiency, cleaner energy use, and increased workforce productivity. Taken together, the results indicate that the accumulation of human capital and innovation in technology cannot only enhance economic growth, but also underpin sustainable economic development.

title: External Debt, Investment, and Financial Development in Botswana and South Africa: A Multivariate Causal Analysis

detail.title: External Debt, Investment, and Financial Development in Botswana and South Africa: A Multivariate Causal Analysis
detail.abstract: This paper employs a multivariate Granger-causality model to evaluate the causal relationship between external debt, financial development, and investment in Botswana and South Africa from 1980-2020. The study includes savings, trade, and economic growth as intermittent variables. Using the autoregressive distributed lag (ARDL) bounds testing approach; empirical results reveal that, for both Botswana and South Africa, there is no distinct short-and long-run Granger-causality relationship between external debt and either financial development and/or investment. However, for Botswana, there is a short-run unidirectional causal relationship from investment to financial development. While for South Africa, the opposite is true. That is, there is a short-run and long-run unidirectional causal relationship from financial development to investment. The policy implication for Botswana is to stimulate the real sector in the short run; immense efforts in promoting investment are recommended. Other results for Botswana support the concurrent promotion of investment, savings, and economic growth because these variables are found to have a short-run and long-run bidirectional causal relationship. For South Africa, it is primarily financial development that drives investment and economic growth. Therefore, policy should promote financial development to stimulate investment, both in the short and long run..

detail.abstract: This study examines the relationship between income levels and key structural factors in Bangladesh, focusing on urbanization, education, female labor force participation, and demographic structure. Using annual time-series data from the World Bank's World Development Indicators for the period 2005-2024, the analysis employs ordinary least squares regression with robust standard errors to assess how these factors are associated with GDP per capita. The results indicate that urbanization, educational participation, female labor force participation, and the working-age population share are all positively associated with income levels, although individual coefficients are not statistically significant at conventional levels due to data limitations. The findings highlight the importance of structural transformation, human capital formation, inclusive labor markets, and demographic conditions in shaping income growth, while emphasizing cautious interpretation and policy relevance rather than causal inference.

title: Assessing The Quality of Education in Rural India: Rankhanda Village as a Case Study

detail.title: Assessing The Quality of Education in Rural India: Rankhanda Village as a Case Study
detail.abstract: "The real India live in villages", this saying is as true today as it was when the country got independence 65 years back. As more than half of the population of the country lives in villages, rural development is an eminent factor for the social and economic transformation .The crucial motivating factor for the development of the economy in today's time is education. India is a country of 1.3 billion people, where 67% of the Indian population lives in rural areas. Approximately 196 million elementary school going children, out of that 146 million are enrolled in rural schools (U-DISE, 2015-16). This research explores the quality of education in rural India, where systemic challenges such as inadequate infrastructure, teacher shortages, and limited access to resources hinder educational progress. It also focused the various initiatives been taken by the government and some of the suggestions for improving the education system in rural or remote areas. Despite government interventions, disparities between rural and urban education are still prevalent. Though the literacy rate has been increased in rural areas but still there is a gap between rural and urban literacy. In addition to that Gross Enrolment Ratio (GER) for girls at both primary and higher secondary level has increased more than that of the boys. A mixed-method approach is employed, combining surveys and interviews of rural population of Rankhanda Village. Quantitative data on literacy rates, school enrollment, and student outcomes all over India is analyzed. The research aims to provide a detailed assessment of the current state of rural education and identifying major barriers. The findings will help inform future efforts to improve teacher training, infrastructure, and technology use, ultimately contributing to more equitable educational outcomes in rural India. The rural India education system needs to improve so as to suit the needs of the 21 st century, taking into consideration of local and global needs.

detail.abstract: The U.S. national security clearance system, governed primarily by SEAD 4 and the “Whole-Person Concept,” is structured around human intent, financial risk, foreign influence, and personal reliability. However, the rapid proliferation of generative AI has introduced a class of risks the framework is structurally unable to address: non-intentional, optimization-driven workflows that result in irreversible data sovereignty loss. This paper argues that “Shadow AI” and Bring-Your-Own-AI behavior create a new insider threat category Optimization-Driven Compromise where cleared personnel inadvertently expose sensitive data to non-sovereign AI systems through routine productivity practices. The analysis highlights the verification gap created by AI data ingestion, logging retention, and the difficulty of post-exposure remediation. It proposes the creation of a new adjudicative category, Guideline N: Cognitive-Digital Hygiene, alongside a modernized penalty matrix, enhanced digital-behavioral monitoring indicators, and structured mitigating conditions such as Zero Data Retention environments and authorized AI sandboxes. The paper concludes that without formal modernization of clearance adjudication and rapid scaling of AI-security talent, the United States faces a quiet but systemic vulnerability one driven not by spies, but by well-intentioned workforce optimization.

title: Arj Samarakoon on Climate Shocks and Eco-Tourism Resilience After Cyclone Ditwah

detail.title: Arj Samarakoon on Climate Shocks and Eco-Tourism Resilience After Cyclone Ditwah
detail.abstract: Eco-tourism has emerged as a key pillar of Sri Lanka's green growth strategy, linking environmental conservation with rural livelihoods. Cyclone Ditwah disrupted this sector by damaging natural assets, access infrastructure, and community based tourism enterprises across eco-sensitive regions. Drawing on climate resilience perspectives articulated by Arj Samarakoon and comparative evidence from emerging economies, this paper examines how climate shocks affect eco-tourism systems and how resilience can be strengthened after extreme weather events. The analysis highlights vulnerabilities exposed by Cyclone Ditwah and proposes policy responses to integrate disaster preparedness, community participation, and green investment into Sri Lanka's eco-tourism recovery framework.

title: Explaining Digital Payments Adoption with Econometrics and Explainable Machine Learning: Cross-Country Evidence from a Global Household Survey

detail.title: Explaining Digital Payments Adoption with Econometrics and Explainable Machine Learning: Cross-Country Evidence from a Global Household Survey

detail.abstract:
This paper studies the determinants of individual adoption of digital payments using the Global Findex Database 2025, released by the World Bank and based on nationally representative household surveys conducted in 2024 across 141 economies. We combine a standard econometric approach with explainable machine learning (ML) methods in order to provide both transparent global benchmarks and granular, policy-relevant insights into digital payment behaviours.

We first estimate a parsimonious logistic regression model on a broad multi-country sample of 5,189 adults from 97 economies, focusing on core socio-demographic and structural characteristics commonly used in the financial inclusion literature. While this baseline specification confirms well-established patterns related to education, income, and access to digital tools, its predictive performance remains limited, as expected given the restricted set of covariates and the objective of cross-country comparability.

We then exploit a richer subsample of 5,183 employed individuals from 74 economies for whom detailed information on digital income reception, payment use cases, and digital connectivity is available. On this enriched sample, we estimate regularized logistic regression, random forest, and gradient boosting models. Predictive performance improves substantially, with the area under the ROC curve increasing from approximately 0.61 in the baseline logit to up to 0.94 in the best-performing ML model. Using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), we show that adoption of digital payments is primarily driven by participation in digital income and payment ecosystems---such as receiving wages, transfers, pensions, or agricultural income digitally, making domestic remittances, and paying merchants and utilities---together with a synthetic index capturing digital connectivity.

Overall, our results illustrate a strong complementarity between traditional econometrics and explainable machine learning. While the econometric model provides an interpretable global benchmark, the ML--SHAP framework uncovers heterogeneous mechanisms that are not captured by standard specifications. These findings have direct implications for the sequencing of digital finance reforms, the design of digital payment strategies, and the transition toward retail central bank digital currencies, particularly in emerging and developing economies.

title: Dollarization Waves: New Evidence from a Comprehensive International Bond Database

detail.title: Dollarization Waves: New Evidence from a Comprehensive International Bond Database

publicationDetails.journalName: Board of Governors: International Finance Discussion Papers (Topic)

detail.abstract: We investigate how the U.S. dollar's prominence in the denomination of international debt securities has evolved in recent decades, using a comprehensive global dataset with far more extensive coverage than datasets used in prior literature. We find no monotonic dollarization or de-dollarization trend; instead, the dollar's share exhibits a wavelike pattern. We document three dollarization waves since the 1960s. The last wave, following the global financial crisis, lifted the dollar's share nearly back to its level at the euro's launch in 2000. Our findings are robust to composition and currency valuation effects as well as alternative data definitions.

title: Multipolar Model as New Configuration of Global Economy: Role and Prospects of BRICS Group
affiliations: Moscow State Institute of International Relations (MGIMO)

detail.title: Multipolar Model as New Configuration of Global Economy: Role and Prospects of BRICS Group
detail.abstract:
A number of structural changes and trends recently observed give signs of the transformation of global economy. Higher contribution of developing countries to the international trade and capital flows, increasingly active processes of economic integration, as well as weakening dominance of the US prove that global economy is facing a shift towards a multipolar model. In this context the future configuration of global economy is a major issue.

The “financial regionalism” scenario, suggested by World Economic Forum in 2009, can be considered as a possible scenario of global economy transformation within the multipolar pattern. This scenario implies formation of three major trade and financial country “blocs”. In general terms this model has been proved feasible based on the comparative analysis of the data observed and the WEF projections, primarily regarding world GDP structure by country groups, as well as the contribution to global economic growth by the corresponding country groups. At the same time the initial configuration within the WEF “financial regionalism” scenario requires certain adjustments taking into account a range of national and regional aspects that are intrinsic to the current state of global economy.

The BRICS group being the leading interregional union of the emerging economies can act as one of the country “blocs” within the scenario suggested. An increasingly high importance of BRICS as a subject of international economic relations relies on its share in global economy and international trade; the recent accession of five new country members is also of great importance. High attractiveness of BRICS for third countries as well as the mechanisms of cooperation adopted by the group also contribute to its significant position in global economy.

title: Diaspora Capital and Flood Response During Cyclone Ditwah: Insights from Arj Samarakoon

detail.title: Diaspora Capital and Flood Response During Cyclone Ditwah: Insights from Arj Samarakoon
detail.abstract: Cyclone Ditwah exposed critical gaps in flood response coordination across Sri Lanka, particularly in the mobilisation of capital, logistics, and verified local implementation. While state institutions remain central to disaster management, the response to Ditwah demonstrated the growing importance of diaspora networks in supplementing public capacity during climate induced emergencies. Drawing on flood response initiatives associated with Arj Samarakoon and comparative disaster governance evidence, this paper examines how diaspora capital functioned as a rapid response asset during Cyclone Ditwah. The analysis situates Sri Lanka within a broader group of climate vulnerable economies where hybrid response models combining public institutions, private capital, and transnational networks have improved speed, transparency, and local impact. The paper proposes an institutional coordination framework to integrate diaspora capital into national flood response systems without undermining state authority.

title: Application of Tree-Based Intelligence Methods for Wind Speed Estimation at the East of Lake Urmia

detail.title: Application of Tree-Based Intelligence Methods for Wind Speed Estimation at the East of Lake Urmia
detail.abstract: Considering the importance of wind in terms of its risks and potentials, the study of this issue is so important. The use of modern intelligence methods is an appropriate approach to predict the wind speed in different regions. East Azerbaijan province is located in the east of Lake Urmia and is one of the windy regions of the country. Due to its proximity to the salt bed resulting from the drying up of Lake Urmia, it is exposed to environmental and health threats. In this study, to predict the wind speed at the target station (Tabriz) using wind speed data from 15 other synoptic stations, Tree-Based intelligence methods including Random Forest (RF), Extra Tree (ET), and M5 models are employed. The monthly wind speed data over eight years (2015–2022) are performed. The 75% of the dataset is considered for the training phase, and the remaining 25% is used for the testing phase. The accuracy and performance of the models in predicting wind speeds at the target station were compared using Pearson's Correlation Coefficient (CC), Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE), and Willmott's Index of Agreement (WI). The results of comparing the models showed that the Random Forest (RF) with CC = 0.74, RMSE = 0.48 m/s, NSE = 0.12, and WI = 0.76 has predicted the wind speed of the Target station (Tabriz synoptic station) with better performance and more accuracy compared to other models.

title: Pompflation: A General Theory of Supply-Side Deflation in the Age of Generative AI

detail.title: Pompflation: A General Theory of Supply-Side Deflation in the Age of Generative AI
detail.abstract: This paper introduces and defines the term "Pompflation": a distinct macroeconomic condition characterized by sustained real GDP growth occurring alongside secular price deflation. While classical economic theory often associates deflation with demand shocks and recessions ("Bad Deflation"), Pompflation describes a supply-side phenomenon driven by the exponential productivity gains of Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI). Applying Wright's Law to cognitive labor, we demonstrate that the marginal cost of intelligence is approaching zero, effectively reversing Baumol's Cost Disease in the services sector. We argue that under Pompflationary conditions, traditional 2% inflation targeting by central banks risks fueling asset bubbles and financial instability. The paper concludes by proposing Nominal GDP (NGDP) targeting as the optimal monetary framework to accommodate this new era of "abundance-driven deflation.

title: Awareness and Prevention of Online Scams Among Elderly Internet Users

detail.title: Awareness and Prevention of Online Scams Among Elderly Internet Users

detail.abstract:
Online scams are a rapidly growing form of cybercrime and represent a serious risk for elderly internet users. Older adults are often more vulnerable due to limited digital skills, high levels of trust in unknown contacts, and lack of access to clear and practical cybersecurity education. As digital services such as online banking, messaging applications, and government platforms become more common, understanding how elderly users interact with online risks becomes increasingly important.

This study examines awareness of online scams, online behavior, and prevention practices among elderly internet users aged 45 years and above in Kazakhstan. A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 52 randomly selected participants from different regions of the country. The questionnaire collected data on demographic characteristics, awareness of online scams, personal experience with fraud, trust in unknown contacts, clicking behavior, use of antivirus software and strong passwords, digital skill levels, and interest in cybersecurity training.

The data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, percentage distributions, cross-tabulation analysis, and a chi-square test to explore relationships between awareness, behavior, and scam experience. The results show that while most respondents actively use the internet, overall awareness of online scams remains limited. Risky behaviors, such as trusting unknown messages and clicking unfamiliar links, were observed even among respondents who reported some level of awareness. Higher digital skill levels were generally associated with safer behavior, but awareness alone did not fully protect users from scam exposure.

The findings also reveal strong interest in short and simple cybersecurity training programs designed specifically for elderly users. This study provides empirical evidence from Kazakhstan, where regional research on elderly online safety is limited. The results highlight the gap between awareness and actual behavior and emphasize the need for practical, behavior-focused, and culturally adapted training interventions to reduce online scam risks among older adults.

detail.abstract: Corruption in public and duciary contracting persists because it is privately negotiated, di cult to prove, and economically pro table. Existing anti-corruption approaches rely on ex post detection, punishment, and moral enforcement, all of which fail to alter incentives at the negotiation stage. This paper proposes a preventive, incentive-compatible system that eliminates pro table corruption by combining blockchain-based cryptographic pre-commitment with contract-speci c corruption insurance. The system forces negotiators to cryptographically commit to all negotiation phases while allowing hidden, non-revealed statements whose existence is immutably timestamped. Any corrupt proposal becomes provable ex post without revealing negotiation contents ex ante. By awarding the entire corruption rent to the rst honest reporter, the mechanism ensures that corruption is a strictly dominated strategy. The model does not rely on surveillance, probabilistic audits, or criminal enforcement, but instead on economic dominance and game-theoretic defection incentives.

title: The Judgment Transparency Principle (JTP) A Foundational Normative Framework for Human-System Interaction

detail.title: The Judgment Transparency Principle (JTP) A Foundational Normative Framework for Human-System Interaction
detail.abstract: As automated systems evolve from passive tools into active agents capable of making decisions, human responsibility is increasingly displaced-not through explicit agreement, but through the imperceptible delegation of judgment. While existing ethical frameworks prioritize explainability (XAI) or fairness, they often fail to address the threshold at which human agency is effectively ceded. This paper introduces the Judgment Transparency Principle (JTP), a normative framework strictly concerning the human-system interface. The JTP asserts that whenever a system influences human actions or outcomes, the existence, boundary, and delegation of judgment must be explicitly perceivable to the user. This principle does not prescribe specific decision logic nor evaluate the correctness of outcomes; rather, it seeks to expose the precise moment when human agency is undermined by the "forgetting" of a decision's delegation. This paper presents the canonical formulation of the JTP to serve as a stable reference point for future technical design, patent implementation, and ethical governance.

We contend that since the 1980 policy reset, the global economic architecture has endogenously transitioned from a "Market Economy"—where labor could realistically convert into capital—to a Subscription-to-Existence Model. In this paradigm, the "Common Man" (P50) is no longer an economic participant but a Biological Annuity whose productivity is siphoned via Inelastic Participation Infrastructures.

Utilizing a forty-five-year longitudinal dataset across six diverse geographical archetypes—the USA (Financialized), Germany (Social-Fiscal), India (Growth-Extractive), China (State-Managed), Sweden (Redistributive-Moat), and the UAE (Pure Rentier)—we perform a distributional autopsy of the median household balance sheet. We introduce the Participatory Insolvency Model (PIM) to prove that while nominal wages at floating prices appear to rise, the Residual Wealth Potential (RWP) of the P50 has been systematically liquidated.

Our findings demonstrate a Symmetry of Extraction: the liquidation of human leisure (Time) and the monetization of the Social Commons (Participation Tolls) have reached their biological limits. We prove that in 2025, the P50 is structurally prohibited from capital formation because the Cantillon Velocity of assets (Housing/Equity) is endogenously calibrated to outrun wage growth by a factor of 4x to 8x. This software artefact (available for universal access at: https://divulgandolasfinanzas-afk.github.io/Divulgando-las-Finanzas-Games/) presents a gamified behavioural intervention and a stochastic model designed to strengthen long-term savings habits amongst the Mexican population. The core methodology employs a strategy of cultural isomorphism, utilising the iconography of Mexican Lucha Libre. 

This approach reduces the cognitive load for vulnerable populations by linking the abstract concept of saving to a culturally recognised combat system. The simulation models the savings lifecycle through a stochastic combat system where "good" and "bad" manoeuvres simulate financial shocks (income variability vs. unexpected expenses), compelling real-time resource allocation decisions. Users progress through three distinct arenas representing savings temporal horizons (Short-Term/Liquidity, Medium-Term/Security, and Long-Term/Capital Accumulation). The system employs adaptive feedback loops and seeks to mitigate hyperbolic discounting biases and foster resilience in long-term planning. This simulation protocol contributes directly to national strategic axes centred on social inclusion, poverty, and inequality.
