title: India Iceberg Index: Measuring AI Occupational Exposure Across 744 Districts

detail.title: India Iceberg Index: Measuring AI Occupational Exposure Across 744 Districts
detail.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence represents a general-purpose technology targeting cognitive capabilities rather than routine manual labor, yet discourse on AI's workforce impact in India remains concentrated on the information technology sector. We introduce the India Iceberg Index, adapting the Project Iceberg methodology to quantify AI occupational exposure across 744 districts and 36 states and union territories using Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) 2023-24 microdata covering 415,549 individuals. Our analysis reveals that approximately 41.5% of India's wage-weighted employment faces technical exposure to currentgeneration AI systems. The national mean Iceberg Index is 37.74 (SD = 9.38) at the district level, with values ranging from 13.41 to 70.56. Critically, visible technology-sector exposure (Surface Index) constitutes only 0.96% of total employment, while hidden cognitive exposure in administrative, financial, and clerical occupations-the "submerged mass"-extends to districts conventionally considered outside AI's reach. Districts exhibiting maximum "surprise" include The Dangs (Gujarat), Central Delhi, and Chitrakoot (Uttar Pradesh), where Iceberg Index values exceed 60 despite near-zero technology-sector presence. Rural areas show higher mean exposure (49.52) than urban areas (31.46), driven by formal administrative employment in government and banking. Industry concentration analysis using the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index reveals that 55.6% of districts exhibit distributed exposure patterns requiring multi-sector policy coordination. These findings challenge the prevailing "tech problem" framing and suggest that India's service-sector development model faces structural vulnerability as AI capabilities expand into entry-level cognitive work.

detail.abstract: Mendoza's wine industry is undergoing a structural crisis that surpasses ordinary economic cycles and exposes a profound deterioration in productive, financial, and territorial sustainability. This article examines how the convergence of overstock, declining consumption, regulatory weakening, market concentration, and financial fragility creates a systemic risk scenario that spreads throughout the entire value chain. Drawing on recent developments-including the flexibilization of the CIU, the expansion of dealcoholized wine, historically low sales levels, and the emergence of significant insolvency proceedings-the analysis highlights the increasing likelihood of contractual breaches and preventive bankruptcy filings. The study contrasts Mendoza's reactive policy responses with the European Union's comprehensive approach, where wine is treated as a strategic territorial, cultural, and socioeconomic asset. It concludes that the absence of robust countercyclical instruments and stable institutional mechanisms, such as a fully operational Wine Bank, exacerbates sectoral fragility and accelerates the diffusion of insolvency risk.

detail.abstract: This white paper examines the increasing legal and political implications of lunar resource extraction and argues that the United States' domestic framework is the most viable and legally sound model for international adoption. This paper contributes to the literature on international space governance by framing lunar resource extraction as a problem of institutional design, property rights, and investment incentives. While the 1967 Outer Space Treaty (OST) prohibits national appropriation of celestial bodies, it remains ambiguous regarding the ownership of extracted resources. This uncertainty leads to a lack of investment and the potential for territorial disputes. By analyzing the Commercial Space Launch Competitiveness Act of 2015, Executive Order 13914, and the Artemis Accords, this paper demonstrates how the U.S. model facilitates resource ownership without asserting sovereignty claims. Drawing on finance and economics perspectives, the research demonstrates why this framework provides the necessary legal clarity and economic incentives to foster international cooperation and private investment, while overcoming the shortcomings of the 1979 Moon Agreement.

detail.abstract: The paper examines the role of technological advances in the long-run growth of real GDP per capita in two European economies (Germany and the United Kingdom) and two Asian economies (China and Japan) between 1993 and 2023. The analytical model is the Solow growth model with exogenous technological progress. Using data from the World Development Indicators on output, investment and population together with Penn World Table 11.0 data on total factor productivity (TFP), the paper creates uniform time series of real GDP per capita, TFP levels and growth rates, investment shares and population growth. The paper compares the roles of technological progress and capital accumulation using descriptive analysis, growth-accounting-style statistics and simple correlation measures. The findings indicate that as compared to the other three economies, the average GDP per capita growth is significantly greater in China because of the rapid expansion of TFP and high shares of investment. In Japan, TFP growth is very weak and its output per person growth is also very low, although investment is rather high. Germany and the United Kingdom are characterized by moderate growth in per capita that is strongly coupled with modest yet positive growth in TFP. Across all four economies, the correlation between TFP growth and GDP per capita growth is extremely high, which reinforces the Solow model's prediction that technological advancement is a key factor contributing to the long-run gains in living standards. The comparative evidence indicates that similar Solow mechanisms are at work in both the advanced and catching-up economies, but that the path taken by technological development differs radically, giving rise to differences in growth experiences.

detail.abstract:
This study investigates the relationship between offshore wind energy development and coastal residential property values, employing New Jersey as a case study during the critical expansion period of 2010-2024. As the United States pursues ambitious renewable energy targets, understanding how offshore wind installations affect nearby communities' economic interests has become increasingly urgent. Despite growing policy relevance, empirical research on property value impacts in the U.S. context remains limited, creating a significant gap in knowledge that this study addresses.

Employing a hedonic pricing framework integrated with a quasi-experimental difference-in-differences design and spatial econometric techniques, this study analyzes 47,832 residential transactions drawn from Zillow ZTRAX data and county assessor records across three New Jersey coastal counties. The methodology addresses spatial autocorrelation, omitted variable bias, and temporal confounders that have limited prior research. Treatment and control groups are defined based on visibility (viewshed) analysis and distance to offshore wind installations, with particular attention to the Ocean Wind 1 project.

Results indicate a statistically significant negative effect of approximately 2.8% on property values for homes within the viewshed of offshore wind developments. The analysis reveals a pronounced distance-decay pattern, with effects concentrated within 15-20 kilometers of installations and dissipating rapidly beyond this threshold. Notably, temporal analysis demonstrates that construction-phase impacts peak at approximately 5.2% but attenuate to roughly 1.5% during the operational phase, suggesting market adaptation over time. Waterfront and ocean-view properties experience disproportionate effects compared to inland coastal properties.

These findings contribute to hedonic pricing theory by documenting how aesthetic externalities from renewable energy infrastructure are capitalized into property values. Practically, the results inform compensation frameworks, setback policies, and community benefit agreements. The evidence suggests that while property value concerns warrant acknowledgment, they should be weighed against substantial climate benefits and may be partially addressed through thoughtful project design and stakeholder engagement.

title: The Social Construction of Wind Energy Risk: A Mixed-Methods Analysis of Community Opposition Formation and Information Dynamics in U.S. Offshore Wind Development

detail.abstract: This explanatory sequential mixed-methods study investigated the social construction of wind energy risk and the formation of community opposition to offshore wind development in the United States, focusing on New Jersey's coastal communities. The research addressed a critical gap in understanding how risk perceptions form and spread in the context of the nation's ambitious offshore wind deployment targets and recent high-profile project cancellations. Grounded in pragmatist epistemology, the study integrated quantitative survey data (N = 412) from coastal residents with qualitative data from semi-structured interviews (n = 28) and social media analysis (7,026 posts). Research questions examined: (a) factors predicting individual-level opposition, (b) information networks and social media dynamics shaping risk perceptions, and (c) the role of procedural justice in acceptance outcomes. Hierarchical multiple regression revealed that the model explained 61.4% of variance in opposition, with visual impact concerns (β = .31), property value concerns (β = .24), and procedural justice perceptions (β = -.24) emerging as the strongest predictors. Findings revealed that offshore wind opposition exhibits a distinctive predictor profile emphasizing visual and property concerns over the health and noise concerns that dominate onshore contexts. Social media has become the primary information source for 93% of interview participants, creating an information ecosystem structurally favoring opposition narratives, with 47.3% of opposition posts containing verifiable misinformation. Procedural justice perceptions partially mediated the relationship between trust in developers and opposition, with 86% of interview participants perceiving engagement processes as performative rather than genuine. The study contributes an Integrated Model of Offshore Wind Opposition Formation (IMOWOF) synthesizing risk perception, procedural justice, place attachment, and information dynamics. Implications include recommendations for enhanced engagement strategies, misinformation counter-messaging, and policy frameworks that address the social dimensions of energy transition. These findings are essential for achieving deployment targets while maintaining democratic legitimacy and community wellbeing.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled export intelligence systems are increasingly used by governments, export promotion agencies, and firms to guide internationalisation decisions. These systems are commonly evaluated using predictive accuracy, expected-value optimisation, and short-term performance metrics. Despite their widespread adoption, export concentration remains persistent in many small open economies, and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) continue to experience irreversible export failure following exposure to regulatory, institutional, or geopolitical shocks. This paper advances the literature by formally operationalising Anti-Fragile Export Intelligence (AFEI) for decision-making under non-ergodic risk, where outcomes are path-dependent, losses are often irreversible, and time averages diverge from ensemble averages. Building on the Export Intelligence Paradox, the paper introduces the AFEI Index (AFEI-I)-a composite metric designed to evaluate how export intelligence systems convert volatility and failure into improved future decision quality. The paper derives testable hypotheses and presents a toy empirical illustration calibrated to the New Zealand export context to demonstrate feasibility using observable organisational and institutional indicators. The framework reframes evaluation away from forecast accuracy toward adaptive learning capacity, with implications for export policy design, AI governance, and productivity strategy in small open economies.

title: The Jurisprudential Evolution of Alternative Dispute Resolution in India: A Critical Analysis of Statutory Frameworks and Judicial Precedents

detail.title: The Jurisprudential Evolution of Alternative Dispute Resolution in India: A Critical Analysis of Statutory Frameworks and Judicial Precedents
detail.abstract: Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) has emerged as a fundamental component of modern justice delivery systems, responding to the growing inefficiencies of traditional litigation. In India, ADR has evolved from a voluntary alternative into a legislatively encouraged and judicially endorsed mechanism for dispute settlement. This article undertakes a comprehensive doctrinal analysis of the jurisprudential development of ADR in India, with particular emphasis on the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. It examines the constitutional foundations of ADR, especially Article 39A of the Constitution of India, and analyses the mandatory nature of judicial referral under Section 8 of the 1996 Act. Through an in-depth examination of landmark Supreme Court judgments such as P. Ananda Gajapati Raju v. P.V.G. Raju and Booz Allen & Hamilton Inc. v. SBI Home Finance Ltd., the article explores the concept of arbitrability and the distinction between rights in personam and rights in rem. The study concludes that Indian jurisprudence has adopted a pro-ADR approach while preserving judicial oversight in matters involving public interest, thereby maintaining a balance between efficiency and justice.

detail.abstract: This paper documents a structural market failure in the deployment of Generative AI: "overuse." We argue that the current "freemium" business model, which reduces the marginal private cost of usage to near zero, functions as a "Reverse Pigouvian tax" that effectively subsidizes the input generating information pollution. We isolate this mechanism through a two-stage research design combining a controlled experiment with a microeconomic model. First, using a dataset of 200 professional accounting tasks and a suite of 17 Large Language Models, we map an empirically derived marginal error cost curve. We find that error rates in dynamic, rule-intensive domains are three times higher than in stable, principle-based domains (61% vs. 20%), with significantly higher economic severity (p < .001). Second, identifying this convex cost structure, we demonstrate that when usage is subsidized and production is opaque, rational agents are incentivized to extend AI usage beyond the social optimum. The findings suggest that without institutional interventions—such as risk-adjusted progressive pricing or strict liability—the decoupling of private benefits from social costs leads to a deadweight loss characterized by systemic resource waste and information degradation.

detail.abstract: We examine the physical anatomy of regulatory arbitrage in global supply chains. Using a novel methodology that isolates ``minimal-processing'' transactions from genuine exports, we find that the rerouting of Chinese goods through Mexico increased by 75 percent following the 2018 US--China trade war. The response is driven by incumbent firms adding tariffed products to their portfolio, is concentrated among differentiated goods, and materializes only under a high tariff wedge. Crucially, we show that this arbitrage drives endogenous investment in physical logistics. Using satellite imagery, we detect a policy-induced expansion in border warehousing, with rerouting firms clustering closer to customs posts than typical exporters.

title: Machine Learning (Deep) Application to Portfolio Allocation

detail.title: Machine Learning (Deep) Application to Portfolio Allocation
detail.abstract: This study presents a broad portfolio optimization model that incorporates advanced deep learning architectures with traditional financial models to improve risk-adjusted performance. Historical data from 2015 to 2023 across a variety of asset classes were used, including equities, Exchange-Traded Funds (ETFs), and bonds. This research further examines the structural capabilities and predictive power of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL), Transformers, and Autoencoders. The suggested models combine covariance estimation, forecasting return, dynamic asset allocation, and dimensionality reduction. Composite models such as Transformer+GNN and Autoencoder+DRL are also explored to leverage both relational and temporal structures in market data. Performance is evaluated through a robust backtesting method, comparing volatility, cumulative return, maximum drawdown, annualized return, and Sharpe ratio across seven strategies, among which are Equal-Weighted, 60/40 allocations, and Mean-Variance Optimization (MVO). Empirical outcomes show that composite learning models demonstrate better stability and risk control, with Transformer+GNN attaining the lowest volatility and drawdown. Mean-Variance Optimization with well-calibrated inputs recorded the maximum cumulative return and Sharpe ratio. Standalone DRL fell short of expectation due to limited structural awareness. The Autoencoder echoed the behaviour of Equal-Weight allocations, which underscores the significance of dynamic policy learning. The results obtained conform to existing literature highlighting the value of relational modeling and feature compression in financial applications. The result of Mean-Variance Optimization in this context challenges previous critiques by establishing that traditional methods retain competitiveness when paired with correct predictive inputs. This study supports the current discourse on data-driven portfolio construction and proposes that the incorporation of deep learning and financial theory can produce robust and adaptive investment strategies. Future study may examine application of latent financial representations within traditional optimization frameworks to further advance robustness and scalability.

Through the estimation of active return, tracking error, and information ratio, using daily data from 35 countries around the world for the period 1990–2024, it is possible to identify the funds that managed to outperform their benchmark rates, reflecting more efficient asset management. The overall results demonstrate that portfolio management worldwide is characterized by a passive approach. This work deepens the understanding of how mutual funds operate and will serve as a guide for investors participating in the stock market.

title: The Party Racism Flip: Media, Moral Narrative, and the Reassignment of Historical Responsibility in American Politics

detail.title: The Party Racism Flip: Media, Moral Narrative, and the Reassignment of Historical Responsibility in American Politics
detail.abstract: This paper examines how racial responsibility has been assigned to American political parties across the full 250-year history of the United States, with particular attention to the period between 1965 and the present. I argue that while racism as an institutional system was historically bipartisan, and, in specific eras, overwhelmingly concentrated within Democraticcontrolled state and local governments (particularly in the post-Reconstruction South), contemporary narratives now portray racism as an inherent and enduring attribute of the Republican Party alone. I contend that this shift cannot be explained solely by voter realignment, policy evolution, or demographic change. Instead, elite media institutions played a decisive role in compressing complex historical patterns into simplified moral identities, projecting Republican racial culpability backward while granting Democrats retrospective moral absolution. This paper distinguishes historical responsibility from narrative legitimacy, traces the evolution of media framing across multiple eras, and evaluates evidence from legislative voting records, public opinion data, and discourse analysis. I conclude that modern racial discourse reflects not a neutral reckoning with history, but a selective moral storytelling process that carries significant risks for democratic trust, historical understanding, and effective reform.

detail.title: Adaptive Intrusion Detection in IoT Networks via Transformer-Based Learning and Dynamic Feature Optimization
detail.abstract: Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS) play a critical role in safeguarding modern network infrastructures against increasingly complex cyber attacks. However, traditional machine learning methods frequently struggle when the data has many features and they require a lot of manual work to select which features are important. To counter this type of problem, our study presented a hybrid deep learning framework and compared three different approaches such as A Baseline CNN-LSTM Attention model with an enhanced CNN-Transformer Encoder Model and a Dynamic Binary Particle Swarm Optimization(PSO) based model for feature selection. This approach uses the NSL-KDD dataset to test the models on different features.The data is prepared using normalization techniques for feature scaling and one-hot encoding to represent categorical attributes numerically.These models were trained such as the first one was baseline hybrid deep learning model,second is Transformer Encoder model, which captures to detect long range dependencies in the data and the third one is PSO Optimized model which works by selecting the most important features to reduce the size of data. The experimental findings revealed that the CNN Transformer Encoder model achieved the best detection performance by reaching the highest accuracy and F1 scores because it can capture relationships across the entire dataset. On the other hand, Dynamic PSO reduces the number of features while maintaining performance. This approach indicates that Transformer Encoder with self attention mechanism and PSO Optimization techniques produce a more robust and efficient IDS for wireless Internet of Things (IoT). The source code used in this study is publicly available at: https://github.com/hassaan145/adaptive-iotintrusion-detection.git.

detail.abstract: Management routinely conveys previously material non-public information to the market during earnings calls, and these disclosures move stock prices. Although communication in this setting is inherently multi-modal, market participants overwhelmingly focus on the words spoken, treating transcripts as sufficient representations of managerial intent and conviction. This paper demonstrates that the voice itself carries a distinct and economically meaningful information channel. Using paralinguistic acoustic features extracted from CEO and CFO speech during the Q&A segments of earnings calls, we show that vocal delivery encodes managerial confidence, stress, and uncertainty in ways that are orthogonal to textual content. Employing an event-study framework, we find that these acoustic signals predict short-and medium-horizon excess returns, indicating that markets do not fully incorporate the information conveyed by voice at the time of disclosure. The results establish the voice channel as a material, under-appreciated component of corporate communication and a systematic under-reaction that is independent of language-based analysis.

title: The Convenience Paradox in Modern Development

detail.title: The Convenience Paradox in Modern Development
detail.abstract: This article examines the central paradox of modern development: while humans expand production and increase material convenience to improve living standards, this very process generates new burdens on the environment, society, and human well-being. Drawing on theories of risk society, energy dissipation in economic processes, and the ecological limits of growth, the study identifies the mechanisms through which sequential chains of consequences emerge, where technological and infrastructural solutions implemented to address existing problems inadvertently create new risks. The article also highlights the rise of digital inequality and the growing pressure of technological adaptation in the context of digital transformation, raising concerns about the absence of a clearly defined developmental end-goal in contemporary societies. Based on this analysis, the study argues for a redefinition of convenience, moving beyond material consumption as the dominant measure of progress and toward a more balanced developmental paradigm grounded in ecological sustainability, social equity, and human reflexive capacity.

detail.abstract:
In today's era of renewed industrial policy — exemplified by major subsidy and tariff programs worldwide — it has returned as a central tool for securing leadership in high technology. However, the current debate about the need to protect potential national industrial leaders leaves open two fundamental questions: when is protection truly justified, and how should it be terminated?
To answer these questions, in this article, I propose a dynamic Ricardian trade model in which productivity growth is limited by a bounded learning curve. In this model, the marginal return to accumulated experience automatically declines as an industry matures. The optimal intervention is a state-contingent Pigouvian wedge (subsidy) that endogenously declines to zero as the learning potential is exhausted. This "sunset mechanism" arises not from administrative decisions, but from the economic nature of diminishing returns to learning.
This model is applied to the global solar PV industry (2000–2024). Estimating a learning rate of 42%, it reveals large timing asymmetry: early Chinese intervention yields sizable welfare benefits, while late EU tariffs have near-zero welfare effect.
The key contribution is an operational rule for time-varying industrial policy that distinguishes welfare-improving dynamic intervention from static rent transfers to mature industries. When learning is bounded, timing is first-order: early intervention pays; late protection does not.

title: Désolé, Monsieur Macron, On N'a Plus de Sous: A Financial Forensic Analysis of the "Missing" Airbus Mega-Order During the 2025 France-China State Visit

detail.title: Désolé, Monsieur Macron, On N'a Plus de Sous: A Financial Forensic Analysis of the "Missing" Airbus Mega-Order During the 2025 France-China State Visit
detail.abstract: During French President Emmanuel Macron's December 2025 state visit to China, expectations of a €50 billion order for 500 Airbus aircraft gave way to a mere administrative "unlocking" of 120 backlog deliveries. Conventional narratives frame this as geopolitical leverage amid EU electric vehicle tariffs. This paper challenges that view, contending that the true constraint is the structural insolvency of China's "Big Three" state-owned airlines (Air China, China Eastern, China Southern). Drawing on November 2025 PMI readings (manufacturing at 49.2 and non-manufacturing at 49.5, both below 50.0) and persistently elevated debt-to-asset ratios averaging around 85%, we argue that the absence of a new mega-order reflects financial necessity rather than strategic choice. In a contracting service economy, additional capital-intensive aircraft acquisitions would exacerbate liquidity risks. The "unlocking" mechanism serves as mutual financial theater: cash flow for Airbus, balance-sheet relief for Chinese carriers. This episode signals the end of China's "checkbook diplomacy" era in civil aviation.

detail.abstract: St. Augustine, Florida—America's oldest city—carries an aura of antiquity far older than its 1565 founding. This speculative essay proposes that the Knights Templar, suppressed in 1312, left an enduring institutional and symbolic legacy through Iberian military orders, crusade-style conquests, Masonic revival, and sacred sites that converged on Florida's coast. Grounded in documented history (Templar suppression, Menéndez's Order of Santiago campaigns, Vatican relic loans) and author fieldwork (Cathedral Basilica crusader murals, St. Johns River markers), the paper distinguishes factual continuities from symbolic patterns and explicit speculation about a Templar-Atlantic relay. St. Augustine emerges as a "preceptory without Templars"—a New World node where crusader logic meets modern Catholic recognition.

detail.abstract:
Accurately forecasting inflation while preserving interpretability remains a central challenge in macroeconomic analysis. Traditional econometric models, though theoretically grounded, often struggle to capture nonlinear interactions and global spillover effects inherent in modern inflation dynamics. At the same time, machine learning models provide superior predictive performance but are frequently criticized for their lack of transparency, limiting their usefulness in policy-oriented settings. This paper proposes an explainable machine learning framework that reconciles predictive accuracy with interpretability in global inflation forecasting.

Using the International Monetary Fund’s Global Inflation Database covering more than 190 countries from 1970 to 2024, we develop a Random Forest regression model incorporating economically motivated features such as lagged inflation, regional average inflation, GDP growth, interest rates, exchange rate indices, and time trends. The Random Forest achieves strong predictive performance, explaining approximately 83% of the variation in global inflation outcomes (R² = 0.829). Feature importance analysis reveals that inflation persistence, captured through lagged inflation, is the dominant driver of future inflation, followed by macroeconomic demand conditions and monetary policy variables.

To address the interpretability limitations of ensemble models, we introduce a global surrogate decision tree trained to approximate the Random Forest’s predictions. While the surrogate does not aim to predict inflation directly, it provides a transparent, rule-based representation of the model’s decision logic and achieves moderate fidelity relative to the Random Forest (R² = 0.417). The resulting structure highlights economically meaningful thresholds associated with inflation persistence, regional spillovers, and macroeconomic regimes.

Overall, this study demonstrates that explainable machine learning can deliver both high predictive accuracy and policy-relevant interpretability in macroeconomic forecasting. The proposed framework offers a practical tool for economists and policymakers seeking to understand the structural drivers of inflation while leveraging the strengths of modern machine learning methods.

title: Energy security: Meaning and implications for Luxembourg in times of transition and geopolitical uncertainty

detail.title: Energy security: Meaning and implications for Luxembourg in times of transition and geopolitical uncertainty
detail.abstract: Energy security is a critical prerequisite for modern economies and societies to prosper and develop. Despite very limited own energy resources, Luxembourg has managed to supply itself securely with oil, gas and electricity for decades. However, energy security has been shaken up over the last couple of years by profound geopolitical changes and uncertainties, such as Russia’s invasion in the Ukraine. Furthermore, the energy transition is often perceived as an element of disorder and a risk to energy security. In stark contrast to this perception, however, it is becoming increasingly clear that the transition is in fact a prerequisite for ensuring energy security. This is particularly true for countries that are highly dependent on energy imports, such as Luxembourg. Nevertheless, in order to turn the transition into a real opportunity with better energy security, a holistic approach is needed addressing far-reaching technical, economic and societal questions. Against the above background, this paper will shed light on energy security in a Luxembourgish context, discussing dependencies and trade-offs as well as risks and opportunities arising from the energy transition and geopolitical uncertainties on a regional, European and global level.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the relationship between Energy Performance Certificate (EPC) ratings and residential property prices in Norway. Drawing on 63,441 single-family home transactions from 2011 to 2024, the study applies a log-linear hedonic pricing framework to estimate the capitalisation of energy performance into housing prices. The relationship between house prices and EPC ratings is estimated using OLS, recursive OLS, and quantile regressions, with additional estimates provided at the municipality level. Statistically significant positive price premiums of up to 13.3 per cent are estimated for dwellings in EPC bands A/B compared to those in band C, while bands D-G are associated with increasing price discounts of up to-26.6 per cent. Recursive estimates highlight the temporal dynamics of these effects, showing that the value premium of energy-efficient homes intensified during periods of high energy prices. Following the energy price shock associated with the war in Ukraine, the premium for the highest efficiency class rose from around 8 per cent to 13 per cent. These findings underscore the importance of energy costs and local market dynamics in shaping the capitalisation of EPCs into housing prices.

detail.abstract: This study examines the price elasticity of demand for mobile data among students, focusing on differences between academic and non-academic usage periods. detail.title: A Field Experiment on How Tracking Consumer Streaks Affects Social Media Usage
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the impact of highlighting streaks-sequences of three or more consecutive behaviors-on consumer behavior through a field experiment with an app designed to reduce social media use. When a user tries to access social media, an intervention interrupts the process, forcing users to indicate whether they want to "resist" or "give in" to using social media. In a six-week experiment (N = 799), we manipulated whether users saw their streaks of resisting and/or giving in as part of the interruption. As hypothesized, highlighting positive streaks of resistance encouraged users to maintain these streaks, whereas highlighting negative streaks of giving in motivated users to break them. Interestingly, while all conditions showed a decrease in social media use, those who had their streaks highlighted showed more frequent attempts to access social media (triggering more overall use) than those who did not, suggesting users strategically engaged with the app to build positive resistance streaks. Nevertheless, these users also reported more favorable attitudes toward the intervention and lower rates of disadoption (which we replicated in a controlled lab experiment), indicating that streak highlighting can be valuable despite its surprising effects. This research contributes to our understanding of how consumers value and respond to gamified feedback; that highlighting streaks can lead to counterproductive behaviors (i.e., more social media use) underscores the need for careful implementation of behavioral tracking.

detail.abstract: This document presents a comprehensive analysis of sound banking principles based on historical evidence spanning over 250 years, mathematical analysis of current Federal Reserve performance, and a detailed framework for monetary reform. The analysis demonstrates that fractional reserve banking operating under sound principles (25% reserves, primary stage lending, commodity backing, personal liability) has proven successful across multiple nations and time periods, while the Federal Reserve system has systematically failed on every stated objective over 111 years of operation. The document provides: (1) Historical evidence from successful sound banking systems (1716-1858) including Suffolk Banking System, Scottish Free Banking, and Canadian banking, (2) Quantitative analysis of Federal Reserve performance (1913-2024), (3) Mathematical proof of current system unsustainability, (4) Detailed reform framework including transition mechanics, (5) International implementation strategy, (6) Responses to common objections. title: The Lonely Robot Problem: Network Effects in Robotics and Industrial Automation

detail.title: The Lonely Robot Problem: Network Effects in Robotics and Industrial Automation
detail.abstract: A robot that works perfectly in isolation may still fail in deployment. This paper introduces the "lonely robot problem": the gap between standalone performance and network-dependent value creation in robotics. Drawing on Chen's (2021) atomic network concept and complementarities theory (Milgrom & Roberts, 1990), I argue that product-market fit metrics mislead robotics strategists when value depends on machine-to-machine interactions. To address this, I propose the Value-Interaction-Density (VID) Framework, a diagnostic tool for evaluating network potential in physical systems. The framework emerged from conversations with robotics founders and product teams, synthesized with existing literature. I apply VID to a hypothetical warehouse robotics scenario and extend it tentatively to agentic AI. The contribution is conceptual; empirical validation is needed. Whether VID predicts adoption outcomes better than capability-focused metrics remains an open question.

VAGE – Value, Architecture, Governance, and Ecosystem 

An Observational Framework for Examining System Readiness
detail.abstract: Across organizations, institutions, and communities, many initiatives struggle not because of lack of effort, intent, or competence, but because the systems supporting them are not structurally prepared for the outcome they seek. While existing frameworks offer valuable guidance on various aspects like strategy, execution, and behavior, repeated failures suggest that certain foundational questions are often left implicit. This paper introduces VAGE (Value, Architecture, Governance, Ecosystem) as an Observational Framework for examining system readiness prior to execution. VAGE does not prescribe solutions or predict outcomes. Instead, it provides a structured way to surface hidden assumptions, misalignment, and constraints that frequently precede breakdowns. Grounded in field experience and informed by established literature in systems thinking, institutional economics, and organizational design, this paper documents the motivation for VAGE, defines its components, positions it relative to commonly used frameworks, and outlines its limitations and potential future applications.

title: The Calm Classroom: Staffing Brief No. 1 --- The Nervous System is Input

detail.title: The Calm Classroom: Staffing Brief No. 1 --- The Nervous System is Input

detail.abstract:
This brief introduces a single boundary for classroom staff: the nervous system provides input, not authority. Signals (speed, intensity, urgency) report change but do not decide meaning or action. Urgency feels like truth but is unreliable for decisions—fast systems inform; slow systems decide.

The analogy: a dashboard light flashes to alert, not to steer. In classrooms, loud moments (emotional, behavioral, or environmental signals) can escalate when treated as immediate commands. Holding the boundary allows delay, reduces words needed, and preserves calm as a valid professional stance.

Key implications when the boundary holds:

  • Escalation slows instead of accelerating.
  • Adults pause rather than rush to explain, diagnose, or correct.
  • Delay becomes legitimate action.
  • Fewer interventions required in the moment.

Optional responses include simple phrases like “I’m noticing a lot of signal. We’re going to slow this down” or “We can decide later.” No script is required; doing nothing (delay) is often sufficient.

This is not a behavior plan, diagnosis, or technique. It names a structural distinction for routing authority under pressure. Signals remain welcome; authority remains separate. No agreement needed—recognition is the goal.

The Calm Classroom series applies a physiological/structural lens to educational settings, focusing on boundaries, signal handling, and institutional capacity for calm under uncertainty. First in the series.

detail.abstract: In the era of rapid development of information technologies and artificial intelligence, traditional macroeconomic indicators-such as GDP, GDP per capita, and export volumes-no longer fully reflect the real intellectual and innovation potential of countries. These indicators primarily measure economic scale and production capacity, while the modern global economy increasingly depends on knowledge creation, innovation efficiency, technological capabilities, and sustainable development. This paper proposes a new multi-capital analytical framework-the Collective Intelligence Index (CII)-which integrates ten key forms of capital: Scientific, Technological, Innovation, IT, Environmental, Creative, Investment, Economic, Human, and Socio-Cultural capital. The study presents a formalized methodology for indicator selection, normalization, and weighting, and discusses the conceptual logic and methodological limitations of the approach. Two complementary levels of assessment are introduced. CII-Intensity reflects the relative efficiency of a national intellectual system on a scale from 0 to 100, while CII-Absolute (CII-Abs) estimates a country's percentage contribution to Global Collective Intelligence (GCI). This separation allows the distinction between intellectual efficiency and absolute scale, eliminating the "large economy bias" inherent in many existing global indices. The proposed methodology enables comparative crosscountry analysis, identification of structural imbalances between efficiency and scale, and formulation of evidence-based policy recommendations for strengthening national intellectual potential. The results demonstrate significant asymmetries between countries and confirm the necessity of developing a new generation of intellectual indicators suitable for the AI-driven and sustainability-oriented global economy.

detail.abstract: We investigate the role of government credit in monetary policy transmission, using detailed credit registry data from Brazil. We find that government direct credit can effectively support small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in a tight monetary policy environment, aligning with developmental objectives. But it comes at the cost of diminishing the overall effectiveness of monetary policy transmission. We also uncover complexities introduced by government-subsidized lending, where the impact of monetary policy transmission is influenced by factors such as credit market segments, lending relationships, and prevailing monetary policy conditions. These insights provide valuable guidance for policymakers on the transmission of monetary policy and the trade-offs involved in government credit programs.

detail.abstract: This paper addresses an emerging problem arising from the shift of digital visibility from search engine rankings to AI-mediated recommendation systems: the inability of many brands to be interpreted by artificial intelligence systems in a consistent, accurate, and trustworthy manner. While existing digital marketing and SEO approaches primarily focus on indexability and ranking, they fall short of explaining how large language models and AI agents interpret, classify, and recommend brands within synthesized responses. The study argues that visibility alone is no longer sufficient for inclusion in AI-driven recommendation spaces and identifies a conceptual gap between being searchable and being recommendable. To address this gap, the paper proposes a conceptual framework that integrates human-centered narrative coherence, machine-interpretable structural signals, and trust-oriented indicators as core components of AI-readable brand identity. The research adopts a qualitative, conceptual methodology based on literature synthesis and analytical observation of AI system behavior. Rather than offering empirical validation, the paper aims to provide a theoretical model that explains how inconsistent signals can lead to misclassification, exclusion, or diminished recommendation likelihood by AI systems. The proposed framework offers practical and theoretical implications for brand strategy, digital visibility planning, and the design of AI-mediated information ecosystems. The paper further illustrates the model through a hypothetical comparison, demonstrating how inconsistent brand signals can undermine AI interpretability despite strong traditional visibility metrics.

detail.abstract: Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), particularly generative AI, have increased public concern regarding the potential displacement of data science professionals. Popular discourse frequently frames AI as a direct substitute for analytical labor, fueling fears of widespread job loss. However, jobs are bundles of tasks, and technological change often reshapes work internally rather than removing occupations outright. This study adopts a task oriented perspective to examine whether AI diffusion corresponds with job displacement or, instead, task reallocation within the data science profession. Using a comparative analysis of U.S. based Data Scientist job postings from a prediffusion baseline derived from a Glassdoor scraped dataset (published in the late 2010s) and a post-diffusion dataset of 2023 postings curated by Luke Barousse, this paper analyzes changes in task and skill related language as proxies for evolving employer expectations. The analysis indicates substantial shifts in the composition of emphasized skills and responsibilities rather than a collapse in demand. In particular, several traditional tools and routine signals have declined in relative share, while signals related to orchestration and modern production workflows have increased. These findings are consistent with a task reallocation framework and motivate task level measurement as a complement to occupation level narratives.

The AI Skills Premium:

Returns To Computer Science Majors In The Chatgpt Era
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether generative AI affected the labor market returns to computer science education. Using American Community Survey data on 3.7 million college-educated workers from 2015-2023, I analyze how ChatGPT's November 2022 launch impacted the Computer Science wage premium. I employ a difference-indifferences approach comparing CS majors to non-STEM graduates before and after ChatGPT.

detail.title: From Ink to Impact: A Comprehensive Analysis of Marketing and Sales Strategies in Book Publishing
detail.abstract: In a country as culturally rich and linguistically diverse as India, the journey of a book from manuscript to marketplace is an intricate interplay of creativity, precision, and strategic planning. This project, titled "Ink to Impact: Designing, ProofReading , Marketing and Publishing of the Book," explores the multifaceted processes that contribute to transforming a literary work into a successful and meaningful product in both national and regional markets-particularly focusing on Maharashtra. Anchored in the dynamic Indian publishing landscape, this study investigates the vital roles of book design, editorial accuracy, marketing innovation, and publishing logistics in determining a book's reach and reception.

title: Licensing Roulette 2025-27: Winning Jurisdictions, Hidden Costs & Next-Wave Growth

detail.title: Licensing Roulette 2025-27: Winning Jurisdictions, Hidden Costs & Next-Wave Growth
detail.abstract: Background: The global online gambling market is projected to expand from US$95.3 billion in 2024 to US$185.17 billion by 2033, driven by technological advancement and market legalization [1]. However, this growth occurs within increasingly complex regulatory frameworks with escalating compliance costs and enforcement actions. Objective: This research analyzes the strategic trade-offs between regulatory prestige, market access, and profitability across global gambling licensing jurisdictions for the 2025-2027 period. Methodology: Comprehensive analysis of regulatory enforcement data, licensing cost structures, tax regimes, and market entry requirements across Tier 1-3 jurisdictions. Data sources include official regulatory body publications, industry reports, and verified enforcement actions from H1 2025.

detail.title: Empirical Research Methodologies in Cybersecurity: Techniques, Applications, and Ethical Considerations
detail.abstract: This paper examines the role and significance of empirical research methodologies in the evolving field of cybersecurity. As cyber threats continue to grow in scale and sophistication, evidence-based research approaches have become essential for evaluating security technologies, understanding user behaviour, and enhancing threat detection and intelligence mechanisms. The study discusses key empirical methods, including observational studies, controlled experiments, surveys, field studies, and data-driven analyses, and explains their relevance in addressing real-world cybersecurity challenges. It further highlights how these methodologies support the assessment of system vulnerabilities, usability of security controls, policy effectiveness, and the performance of artificial intelligence and machine learning-based security solutions. In addition, the paper addresses critical ethical considerations such as data privacy, informed consent, responsible disclosure, and regulatory compliance, which are central to conducting trustworthy cybersecurity research. By identifying practical challenges related to data accessibility, reproducibility, and the dynamic threat landscape, this study underscores the need for rigorous and ethically grounded empirical research. Overall, the paper provides a structured overview that can guide researchers and practitioners in designing reliable, impactful, and responsible cybersecurity studies.

title: From Large Language Models (LLMs) to Large Understanding Models (LUMs): A Paradigm Shift for AI Understanding and Organizational Decision-Making

detail.title: From Large Language Models (LLMs) to Large Understanding Models (LUMs): A Paradigm Shift for AI Understanding and Organizational Decision-Making
detail.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have transformed how artificial intelligence processes and generates human language. Despite their impressive achievements, these systems remain fundamentally constrained by statistical association, limited semantic grounding, and opaque internal mechanisms[1]. Agentic AI architectures-which extend LLMs with tools, planning, and autonomous task execution-expand operational capacity but inherit the same limitations, failing to provide the transparency, causality, or predictive reliability required for next-generation decision intelligence[2]. This paper introduces Large Understanding Models (LUMs) as a novel framework that integrates semantic comprehension, causal inference, contextual reasoning, and explainable predictive actions into a unified architecture[3]. A formal mathematical modulation is proposed to quantify the advantages of LUMs over LLM-based and agentic systems in terms of understanding quality and decision precision. LUMs are presented as a foundational paradigm for advancing trustworthy, explainable, and contextually aligned AI, with broad implications for organizational decision-making and AI governance.

detail.title: KavitaKunj: Marathi Poem Generational Platform
detail.abstract: The study presents KavitaKunj, an AI-powered Marathi poem generation platform that integrates artificial intelligence with regional literature to promote language preservation and creative expression. With the increasing dominance of English and other high-resource languages in the digital domain, Marathi-despite its rich literary heritage-faces challenges in maintaining cultural relevance among modern audiences. KavitaKunj addresses this gap by leveraging a fine-tuned MarathiGPT model, trained on a diverse dataset of classical and contemporary Marathi poems. This model enables the generation of meaningful, thematically coherent poetic verses based on user-provided prompts. The platform not only encourages literary engagement but also offers new avenues for educational use, cultural enrichment, and AI-driven creativity. The research emphasizes the need for inclusive NLP development that supports underrepresented languages in the AI space. Through KavitaKunj, the study demonstrates how technology can bridge the gap between tradition and innovation, ensuring the continued evolution of regional languages in a rapidly digitalizing world.

detail.abstract: Amidst escalating regulatory complexity and cyber threats, existing RegTech solutions often remain confined to reactive monitoring via dashboards, failing to integrate predictive intelligence for proactive decision-making and systemic resilience. This gap leaves enterprises vulnerable to compliance failures that cascade into broader financial instability and critical infrastructure disruptions. This working paper addresses this shortfall by proposing the “From Dashboards to Decisions Framework (D2D Framework)” which is a novel maturity model that formalizes the progression of AI-driven regulatory intelligence (RegIntel) from passive visualization to orchestrated, resilience-enhancing decisions. The D2D Framework outlines five maturity levels, core capabilities, and integration pathways, enabling enterprises to link regulatory compliance directly to operational and national-scale resilience metrics. Drawing on a synthesis of RegTech trends, the paper demonstrates how this framework reduces compliance costs by 30-50%, mitigates systemic risks, and supports critical infrastructure protection. Challenges such as AI bias and explainability are examined, with recommendations for ethical implementation. Beyond individual enterprises, the D2D Framework contributes to national interests by fostering scalable systems for financial stability and cyber resilience in an interconnected global economy. This conceptual framework paper provides a blueprint for researchers and practitioners to advance RegTech toward proactive, secure enterprise architectures.

title: AI-Driven Dynamic Pricing: Transparency and Ethical Implications
affiliations: KEDGE Business School and University of Waterloo - Department of Management Sciences

detail.title: AI-Driven Dynamic Pricing: Transparency and Ethical Implications
detail.abstract: This article explores transparency in AI-driven dynamic pricing, a strategy that uses advanced algorithms and real-time data to adjust prices in digital markets. Although researchers have extensively studied dynamic pricing and artificial intelligence, the ethical aspects of algorithmic opacity and the limitations of current fairness and trust theories remains unexplored. To address this gap, we develop a conceptual framework that incorporates signaling, fairness, and trust theories to explain how transparency can balance efficiency with ethical accountability in AI-driven pricing. We analyze algorithm disclosure practices, data-driven decision criteria, and consumer responses to clarify transparent pricing mechanisms. Our conceptual framework shows that increased transparency enhances perceived fairness and ethical trust, promoting sustainable consumer engagement and reducing risks of discriminatory pricing. Our research offers a foundation for rethinking AI pricing, urging policymakers and industry leaders to prioritize transparent, ethical practices in the digital markets.

title: Shock Amplification and Delayed Recovery in Resource Economies: The Role of Extraction Costs
affiliations: Université Laval - Département d'Économique and Université Laval

detail.title: Shock Amplification and Delayed Recovery in Resource Economies: The Role of Extraction Costs
detail.abstract: This paper shows how production-cost heterogeneity amplifies both the contraction and recovery dynamics of resource-based economies during global commodity price shocks. A simple framework predicts that high-cost producers face steeper declines in output and investment during downturns, and more sluggish recoveries due to deeper investment withholding and slower capacity rebound. We test these predictions using the 2014–2016 oil price collapse, comparing Alberta—one of the world’s highest-cost oil producers—to a synthetic control constructed from lower-cost jurisdictions. Alberta experienced significantly sharper declines in hydrocarbon output, investment, and per capita GDP, and a more prolonged recovery—consistent with structural amplification and dynamic hysteresis. A cross-jurisdiction event study and a focused comparison with Saskatchewan, a nearby lower-cost producer, reinforce these findings. Placebo, leave-one-out, and backdating tests confirm robustness. The results highlight a dynamic, structural channel of asymmetric shock transmission and demonstrate how cost heterogeneity shapes macroeconomic resilience in resource-dependent settings.
